#4216. Trees Hate You Review: You’ll Enjoy Hating Them Back

Trees Hate You uses unpredictable traps and cartoon-style humor in a short, silly rage game, though its bugs and limited challenge may frustrate some.

It’s a very odd time in gaming where we’re seeing a lot more games coming out than ever before. Some are better than others, but many seem to simply have some fun and interesting premises that draw you in.

One such game would be Trees Hate You, which is a ridiculous rage game about being targeted by trees. Sounds like it shouldn’t be very good, but surprisingly the game’s Looney Tunes-esque approach to mechanics makes it an enjoyable game.

I played the game for around four hours, though a speed run could be significantly quicker, and came away enjoying most of my time with the game. It isn’t a perfect game, but it is a fun game, especially if you’re just looking for a silly little rage game.

It’s not a complex or complicated game in all reality, but that’s part of its charm. You play as a person who’s being hunted by trees for some reason or another and must navigate through several locations to finally reach your destination.

There’s very little in the way of story since virtually all of the information presented is through the visuals of the game. You’ll need to make your way through many dangerous traps that will change, sometimes seemingly at random.

It isn’t a perfect game, but it is a fun game, especially if you’re just looking for a silly little rage game.

There are four “levels,” three of which are separated into smaller sections to make it more digestible. Each section has a central theme and introduces some new trees while finding creative ways to make you scream obscenities.

It’s a pretty short and sweet game that culminates in a very, very odd ending. There aren’t really any abilities to get or anything to make the game easier. From the outset of the game, you’ve got your movement buttons and whatever brain power you can muster.

Super Meat Boy 3D is still the same series you love, now with even more ways and directions to die over and over. Here's our full review!

For a lot of rage games, each section of the game is stagnant so that you can learn from your mistakes and grow smarter. In this game, that entire ideology is completely thrown out the window, and it makes it much more interesting to play.

For almost every section of the game, when you die you end up back at the last checkpoint, but you’ll notice that something might be a little different. Sometimes it’s a new tree popping up along the path or a new path entirely.

This seemed to change at random upon death, and figuring out how to handle the changes added a new layer to the game. For some, it’s going to be frustrating in a different way, since it does change, meaning memorizing the path isn’t particularly helpful.

I thoroughly enjoyed that change of pace. As a big fan of great roguelikes, seeing that sort of game design appear here gave me pause at first until I got used to it. It managed to keep the game fresh despite the short run time.

There was a lot about this game that I thoroughly enjoyed, but there is no denying that the game felt way too short. Perhaps that was because I simply had played through some other rage games recently that prepared me for this, but still I felt it could’ve been a much longer experience.

Being a short experience isn’t too bad, as there are a few things that you can grind for if you really want, such as coins and hats, but at the end of the day this is a game you could beat in a single session. I suppose I was hoping to have a bit more oomph out of the game, though what we did get was more than fine.

There is a challenge mode that changes up some of the levels and makes things a bit more complicated with more traps and threats, but the levels will always remain the same between deaths. It was nice to provide the option to give players more bang for their buck.

The game doesn’t really waste any time on things that aren’t humorous or torturing you, which is a big bonus. As I approached the end, though, I had hoped the game would surprise me and get a bit longer or more ridiculous, but there was no such luck.

If you're looking for experiences that aren't artificially prolonged, check out these ten fastest Metroidvanias to 100%.

Video games are not often known for their sense of humor, and even less so for their ability to utilize visual gags. Trees Hate You has decided to right this wrong by making what effectively feels like a Looney Tunes episode into an entire game.

At first it was just some slight things, moments that felt naturally funny because of the tension and ridiculousness of the game. That changed after a few levels when trees began to do whatever they pleased, seemingly just to mess with me.

There is one tree in particular that embodies this ideology entirely. One tree blocks your path early on in the game by bending at insane angles to force you in another direction. This same tree will do this for the entirety of the game.

You’ll come across a path sometime later, and suddenly out of the sky the tree will reach down and block your path. This was incredibly idiotic and amazing. I had to stop and try it again just to make sure I could see what exactly was going on.

It’s a pretty hilarious game, especially when you run into those annoyingly funny moments that make you feel like you’ve been outsmarted by the trees. Even if you’re not a big fan of this kind of humor, it’s still enjoyable to see all the unique ways the trees manage to get you.

This is going to be something that I think gets to be a little divisive amongst people who play the game. On the one hand, the game isn’t quite as difficult as it could be, but on the other hand, the changing mechanics could make it more difficult for some.

I would’ve liked to see the game be a bit more difficult the first go around, but there is a challenge mode. It sort of balances out, giving everyone a chance to enjoy something about the game, but there were only a few sections that really got to me.

It’s a pretty hilarious game, especially when you run into those annoyingly funny moments that make you feel like you’ve been outsmarted by the trees.

It feels like the game is more about trial and error rather than conquering any difficult mechanics, and that’s more than okay, but it does take away some of the feeling of accomplishment. In reality, it feels like the game is more designed to watch others fail than to be played itself.

Ironically, there’s a lot of time to sit with what happens when you die in some crazy fashion. You’ll respawn at a checkpoint with virtually no risk, meaning you’ll never need to complete a past section a second time.

Trees Hate You is an interesting rage game that leans more heavily into the absurdity of the genre than the actual rage. Still, it’s a hilarious and ridiculously fun game. You’re going to walk away from the game having enjoyed yourself immensely despite some of the more pressing issues. There are annoying bugs that will force you to start from a prior checkpoint, but all in all, the game is a very good time.

#4215. Interview: Honkai Star Rail lead designer talks epic Aeons and lasting memories aboard the Astral Express

Only good things to come for Trailblazers out there

If you haven't been keeping up with the latest, you should know that Honkai: Star Rail's recently launched update is massive in more ways than one. The RPG has been making waves since it launched, and for good reason - one of the main ones is the fact that its narrative is, as my own brother puts it, "just so, so good".

Obviously, it's not just him who's enamoured with the deep lore of Honkai: Star Rail, as HoYoverse's space fantasy adventure is happily enjoying over 10 million downloads on Google Play alone. It's hard to believe it's been three years since it launched - I still fondly remember how much I enjoyed giving it a go in its early access phase way back when.

Now, with its Planarcadia arc drawing to a close, it's only fitting that we peek behind the curtain to see the inner workings of this epic tale - something we luckily got the chance to do over at the HoYoverse Media Tour 2026 in Seoul (answers have been edited for clarity and brevity).

During the roundtable interview with ChengNan An, Lead Game Designer of Honkai: Star Rail, we learned more about Version 4.7 - particularly Aha, the God of all Elations, which is also what ChengNan An says he is most excited for. For the uninitiated, Aeons are the Ultimate Beings here, and with the arrival of Aha, everyone will finally get the very first playable Aeon.

Apart from that, there are also more exciting things to look forward to over the horizon. "We started a new design to break free from the limit of the 4-character team to bring players a fresh experience. This allows you to create different team combinations, strategies, and options in battle, providing a sense of novelty."

It was nice to hear how the team is continuously improving on the combat elements too, especially since Honkai: Star Rail has such a robust turn-based battle system (which I really appreciate!). "Looking at the history of turn-based games, we see that it's already been well-loved by players for a long time. The team is a big fan of turn-based games, so we learned from the classics of the genre and realised that there's room for expansion there. We also created something more story-driven but still builds upon the action of Honkai Impact 3rd. We're so glad that players are rediscovering the charm of turn-based combat, and we're happy to be a part of it!"

Major updates for the latest version include reward stages as well, and with all these new additions, the notion of keeping things balanced for newbies and veterans remains the same. "In the future, we will also look for more ways to reduce our players' burdens while playing," he says.

That's actually something I've always been curious about -  live service games are a huge challenge, so how can the team give HSR lasting power and yet make sure it stays accessible to new players who might be intimidated by the RPG and its deep lore?

"Ever since Honkai: Star Rail's launch, we have been continuously looking into how to provide our players with fresh experiences while keeping the barrier to entry low. Shortly after the launch, we already added some quality-of-life designs to help our players have more flexible options," he explains. "We also have features that help players get into the storyline more easily, or they can accelerate the dialogue if they want to. They can also get into the latest content without worrying too much about the prerequisite quests. More importantly, we always need to introduce something new for our players, such as Aha and the new gameplay modes."

This goes hand-in-hand with the entire planning process that also takes into consideration all kinds of player feedback. "We always try to balance long-term planning and instant changes too," he adds.

Obviously, this includes improvements not just within the game itself but also in how it runs, particularly with mobile devices getting far more advanced as the years go by (and file sizes getting bigger and bigger). I did have to bring up the inevitability of the iPhone Duo, which they're already on top of. "We keep improving our game to adapt to modern platforms, and in terms of the iPhone Duo, we already received the requirements for adaptation, so stay tuned for more info on that!"

Based on everything I learned at the interview, at the end of the day, what keeps the fire burning for Honkai: Star Rail, in my opinion, is the fervent passion that the entire team has for bringing emotional stories to players - true to the Honkai brand. ChengNan An echoes this.

"We work together to give our players lasting memories, so what I enjoy most is when, after all our efforts, we finally see the highlights of the storyline or the characters in-game, and that moment is what I enjoy most, along with seeing players react to how they've been impacted by the game. The characters give them a new perspective on how to tackle difficulties in the real world. They find a way to live a better life, and that's the most touching moment."

And before we wrap up, he shares his wishes for the community moving forward. "Honkai: Star Rail is a journey that continues throughout different planets, and for our development team, it is also a journey of exploration. We strive to keep giving players surprises through stories, characters, and game modes," he concludes. "We want to give players lots of memories to look back on, so that years down the line, they'll recall that one person or that one moment they experienced, and that will bring them joy."

It's safe to say that things are only going to get better from here, especially with such a dedicated and inspiring team giving the RPG their all. So, full steam ahead for the Astral Express!

#4214. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 6, 2026

This week and weekend is all about the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, one of the few games I feel deserves the title of masterpiece. And the remake is really well done! I got every heart piece, every Gold Skulltala, the Goron Sword, and the biggest pouch for every one of my items over the course of the review... but I am contemplating jumping right back in for another go.

We also revealed our next cover and in case you missed the announcement it is... pause for effect... Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis! It's an awesome cover that celebrates the history of Lara Croft, and along with a cover story on the game, we also have a big retrospective on the series. I highly recommend subscribing to get your issue if you haven't already.

But it wasn't all just Zelda and Tomb Raider this week. Below you will find a list of weekend play recommendations, but before that... some of our biggest stories of the week.

We have been writing a lot about The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time remake this week because it is one of 2026's most exciting games, and it's real good. The remake is not particularly surprising. It mostly sticks to the trajectory of the original game, but there is a reason it is considered one of the best games of all time. It also looks and plays amazing.

You can read the full review here (or watch the video above), but we also have a big interview with the game's producers (one of whom worked on the original Ocarina of Time, and one who directed Breath of the Wild among many other Zelda games), some details about the Easter Eggs that did and did not make it into the remake, and a very handy tip for the game if you happen to be playing with a Switch 2 Pro controller.

World of Warcraft: Forever is out now and it’s a great time to jump into the revamped and expanded version of a project that changed online games forever back in 2004. A thousand new quests, multiple new zones, countless revamps, and an impressively stunning visual overhaul make it the perfect time to jump in for anyone who’s ever been curious to explore Azeroth.

2022's Escape Academy was a sneaky little puzzle game that surprised me and its sequel released this week. Taking place in a school obsessed with puzzles, you play as a student who must make their way through a series of escape rooms. The puzzles are clever, and the setting is charming, but the secret weapon is the local, split-screen co-op. Solving puzzles together is fun especially when one player needs to look at one section of a room to help dictate a solution on the other side of the room. My wife and I both love video games, but rarely play co-op games together just because of our disparate, individual tastes. But Escape Room is one we enjoyed together and we're so far enjoying the sequel. My only complaint so far is... I wish it ran a little better.

While we collectively use the term here for the sake of familiarity, I’m always a bit hesitant in my own mind to label a game under the wide banner of “Metroidvania.” In part, that’s because I think the two referenced games (Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night) are actually more different than they might appear at first glance. Gloomsoft’s recent release, Moadra, recognizes that distinction, crafting a game that draws heavy inspiration from the specific tradition of Super Metroid, even while presenting an intriguing and atmospheric fiction that is great fun to discover. In movement, actions, and exploration, Moadra feels remarkably similar to  the best of the 2D Metroid games. A scanning tool also leans into the Metroid inspirations, revealing details about the weird alien world you’re navigating. If you’ve been hungry for a game that scratches that particular itch of sci-fi gear/ability-gated exploration, I think you’ll find a lot to love in this game.

I get the Marvel fatigue we've all been experiencing. There are a lot of games and a lot of movies and a lot of TV shows and many are good, but lately most feel like homework. For those reasons, you'd be forgiven for dismissing the 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy game, but I promise you it is good. For one, it is standalone. It does not directly tie to any specific Marvel media. No homework necessary. And for two, it's just a really good game with an affecting story and a unique take on the characters that most of us met for the first time in the movies. And, for the BioWare fans out there mourning the loss of Mass Effect, this game has some Mass Effect energy. It's available on Switch 2 this week and I happily recommend it, especially if you missed it five years ago.

This exclusively two-player board game features a fun mix of activities. You act as both a dungeon architect, and an adventurer delving into said dungeons. Each player creates their own version of a challenging dungeon filled with traps, monsters, and treasures.

But you’re also forced to take on the dangers of your opponent’s crafted dungeon, to see who manages to come out on top. If you have fond memories of the hidden-info nature of old games like Battleship, but you want some greater strategic depth and fantasy flavor thrown in, this one is a great pick.

#4213. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.

After Nintendo's reveal this week that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time had shifted 5.2 million units in its first four days, it will come as no surprise to hear that it's a smash hit in Japan. But still, Famitsu's latest numbers are in, and the physical is flying!

According to this week's chart, Link's latest produced ~537,000 physical sales in its chart debut — giving it the lion's share of Japan's 810,000 sales that Nintendo reported, and leaving around 273,000 sales for digital. As we say, it's hardly surprising, but still!

It makes all the other entries this week look piddly by comparison. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and Rhythm Heaven Groove round out the podium with a comparatively tiny 16,621 and 8,793 sales, respectively, and Stellar Blade: Complete Edition made its debut in fourth.

While Switch 2 sales are actually down following last week's bump, the console still leads this week's hardware chart by a comfortable margin. Nintendo's latest pulled in an additional ~53,000 sales this week, topping the PS5 Digital Edition, which came in with 11,377.

Once again, however, those Digital Edition sales swing things in Sony's favour over the Switch 1 when we look at the total SKU numbers for the week. The three PS5 systems combined this time for 11,699, while the Switch 1 units came in at 5,148.

#4210. A.O.T 3 Final Preview: Possibly Shaping Up To Be One of the Best Anime Adaptation Video Games

This is DualShockers' preview of Attack on Titan 3, the penultimate entry in the AOT Video Game series developed by Omega Force and published by Koei Tecmo.

The Attack on Titan series by Hajime Isayama is genuinely one of the most important works for fans worldwide. The show has sparked a massive debate over its controversial ending, but putting that aside, you can’t argue with its overall impact: brilliant storytelling and action that fans will remember for ages.

DualShockers played A.O.T. 3 at a preview event, slashing Titans and humans alike, with the entirety of Attack on Titan's story being adapted.

And now, eight years after the last game in the franchise, Koei Tecmo’s Omega Force is back with Attack on Titan 3. The full game launches next month in December on the PS5, Xbox Series X and S, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2. At DualShockers, we had the opportunity to check out a final preview build, and I must say, as a veteran fan of both the series and the games, they’re truly going out swinging on this one.

One of the biggest changes in Attack on Titan 3 is how it approaches its storytelling. You see, back then there was this evident problem that Omega Force could only adapt parts of the story since the anime was still airing, which meant that you weren’t going to get the full package, or at least, where the manga had reached in contrast to the show.

With AOT3, it still remains true to the storytelling presentation of the prior entries. But rather than simply allowing you to relive the anime's biggest moments through the familiar cast, this game once again introduces an original character for you to create and customize.

Our OC character suffers a devastating loss after their previous squad is wiped out during a Titan encounter beyond the walls. So, after developing a fear of Titans from the incident, they're removed from active duty and assigned to instruct the 104th Cadet Corps. This gives you a chance to interact with familiar faces such as Eren, Armin, and Mikasa before eventually graduating from the instructor role and taking command of your own reconnaissance squad.

This approach is very promising because it gives Omega Force a chance to explore parts of the Attack on Titan universe that don't necessarily receive the same attention in the anime. You're not another member of Eren's generation experiencing everything alongside him. But instead, you're an experienced soldier watching these young cadets grow into the people who will eventually shape humanity's fate.

There are also original story events and character interactions designed to expand on the relationships between your character and the existing cast, which is a very nice gesture for us longtime fans if we want something new from this whole experience, especially for characters that didn’t get a ton of screen time in the main show or earlier seasons.

DualShockers spoke to A.O.T. 3 producer Hideo Suzuki about the new Titans, balancing grittiness with arcade action, and why there's no romance.

Of course, none of this hard work over the past 8 years would matter nearly as much without the one thing that makes AOT such an exciting property to adapt into a video game: its combat.

Fortunately, Omega Force hasn't simply brought back the same Omni-Directional Mobility (ODM) system from Attack on Titan 2 and called it a day. The studio has made several adjustments to how you can move around the battlefield, giving the familiar grappling mechanics far more flexibility while also adding new layers of strategy to Titan encounters.

Previously, much of the combat revolved around attaching your ODM anchors to a Titan, reeling yourself towards it, and timing your attack to strike its nape. While that foundation remains intact, AOT3 has generally put more emphasis on identifying weaknesses before committing to an attack. The gameplay rhythm now feels more like a hybrid between a strategic action game.

You can now target individual body parts, allowing you to damage limbs, interrupt attacks, and temporarily immobilize Titans before going for the finishing blow. This is especially important because these guys are much more aggressive, with new attack patterns that require you to watch their movements rather than blindly rush toward their weak spots.

One of the biggest changes in Attack on Titan 3 is how it approaches its storytelling.

Other noticeably uplifting additions include the maneuverability upgrades and defensive options. You can attach yourself to certain surfaces to reposition, use boost jumps to gain additional height, and even dive or slide along the ground to avoid incoming attacks, which is very useful when dealing with larger Titans during their one-on-one boss fight encounters where you have to stun them for the one-hit kill from their nape area.

As for defensive mechanics, you can use well-timed dodges and parries to defend against incoming attacks. Combat Arts also add another layer of progression, giving you access to powerful unlockable special attacks as you increase your military rank. It's an ambitious evolution of the combat from the prior entries, one that I’m very excited to experience to a greater extent with the full release.

The overall game’s flow looks extremely ambitious, and what I mean is that the game has three working gears in motion for the full package here: interacting with your squadmates at the base, the main story missions that progress the campaign, and your Exterior missions.

The latter is one of the highlights, as it lets you freely explore the world with your squad in tow to hunt down more Titans and fulfil different requests from NPCs you come across. It’s essentially a way to give you more gameplay freedom instead of railroading you from start to finish to showcase the anime's main story, and doing Exterior missions also lets you reap additional rewards and useful upgrade materials, which you definitely need and can’t skip since they let you enhance your equipment.

And speaking of gameplay freedom, you can put any doubts to rest about whether you can jump into this game without prior experience with how the first two games worked. There are a bunch of accessibility and control scheme options that let any player easily enjoy the story, but if you want total control, you can turn off any options that automate the combat mechanics, which I honestly prefer since you’re way more vulnerable to mistakes that way, and it makes the game more punishing.

Still, I can promise you that Attack on Titan 3 is genuinely worth having on your radar for the December releases. With how much I got to sample here, I can’t wait to see how more of the character interactions play out, how the talent points fully work with everything in place, along with how the noteworthy battles in the show play out here, and that includes the whole sections of Marley from Season 4 and beyond. It is a lot to look forward to on my side, but I’ll gladly march into battle head-on with my goth Scout Corps Captain.

This list discusses the best Anime-inspired action games that capture the genre far better than SAO: Echoes of Aincrad.

#4209. Genshin Impact fans on PS4 only have six weeks to find another platform as support winds down with one final update

Premium in-game purchases have now been disabled on PlayStation 4, as one of Genshin's four original launch platforms prepares to get dropped in early April.

Version Luna 5 of Genshin Impact is now live, but it's a bittersweet occasion for fans of HoYoverse's breakout gacha RPG – at the very least, those who are still playing the game on PlayStation 4, which is presumably true of somebody out there.

HoYoverse announced last year that they intended to wind down support for Genshin Impact on PS4, which – alongside PC, Android, and iOS – was one of the launch platforms for the game back in 2020. And with Version Luna 5, those end days are upon us.

The game has already been delisted on the platform since last September, meaning it was no longer available for download and could only be updated by players who already had it installed. But as of today, paid purchases from the in-game store have been disabled on PS4; and in six weeks' time, on approximately April 8, Version Luna 6 will discontinue access to the PS4 version altogether.

In many ways this is unsurprising – Genshin is already available on both PS5 and Xbox Series to sate fans eager to play on console, and the PS4's hardware is increasingly struggling to keep up with this massive open-world game after more than five years of regular updates have ballooned both its file size and technical requirements.

Aptly enough, Luna 5 takes the main story action back to the nation of Mondstadt, the location where the Traveler (and, by extension, the players) took their first steps into the world of Teyvat back in September 2020. It feels like a symbolic last hurrah for the original console home of the game, as does the inclusion of a Chronicled Wish banner focussing on some of Mondstadt's most iconic (read: too old to be meta by now) 5-Star characters – namely Eula, Mona, Albedo, Klee, Diluc, and Jean.

And as the icing on the Tea Break Pancake, this banner is running alongside the long-anticipated introduction of Varka – the Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius who has been a major character in the game's lore from the very beginning, but who only became playable with today's update.

Looking ahead to that post-Luna 6 future, Genshin Impact will still be available on PS5, as well as Xbox Series consoles, PC, and mobile devices – so hopefully anyone who is still playing primarily on PS4 will find another platform they can continue the adventure on by April.

#4207. The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin may be your next anime gacha obsession, with a hint of Ghibli, and this latest trailer may be what sells you on it

There's another free-to-play action RPG very much on the horizon. Will this be the one to win you over?

It seems like we’re getting one of these every few months, but the world of mobile action RPGs that look like the games that, just a few years back, were only possible on consoles is expanding with another new entry.

Netmarble, a studio and publisher known for its free-to-play games on mobile and PC, recently unveiled the launch date for The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin, its next major release that’s very much coming for the Genshin Impact crowd.

The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin is an open-world action RPG based on the world of The Seven Deadly Sins anime and manga. The game takes place in the world of Britannia, which looks similar to the way it does in the anime.

That said, the story of the game is not based on the anime or manga, Instead, it’s an original story set in the universe of the show. You play as Prince Tristan of the Kingdom of Liones who must find a way to bring order back to Britannia.

The gameplay should be familiar to anyone who played a free-to-play action RPG in the last decade. It features action combat, a roster of diverse heroes that you assemble to form teams, and a large pretty world to explore where you’ll also get to meet new characters.

Speaking of which, while Origin has its own original story, expect to be teaming up with characters from the series - some of whom wouldn't be able to meet naturally. You can thank the game's multiversal story for that.

Beyond all the serious business of saving the world and battling monsters, The Seven Deadly Sins: Origin also has a cozy, relaxing side. You’ll be able to fish, cook, forage and take on the beauty of the world with your pals.

The game has a bit of an unusual release schedule. It’s set to arrive on PC, PS5, iOS, and Android. PC (Steam), and PS5 players will be able to jump in starting March 16, whereas the global mobile launch is scheduled for one week later, on March 23.

You can pre-register right now on the official website if you’re interested in earning a few rewards when the game launches. You can, of course, always wishlist the game on Steam and the PlayStation Store, too.

#4205. 10 Best Soulslikes With Fluid Movement Mechanics

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

Soulslikes represent a subgenre of ARPGs with quite distinct characteristics, including various constraints intended to establish their aggressive and challenging nature.

Features such as combat that prioritize functionality over spectacle, as well as limited and mundane traversal methods, are a constant among Soulsborne games' descendants, precisely because they exploit these limitations to create immersive experiences.

It's an incredibly delicate balance because, if poorly executed, it leads to clunky campaigns where the mere act of moving from one place to another can become tedious, though there are also exceptions that prove the rule.

Therefore, in order to shed light on these anomalies and draw on the contributions of titles with a lighter approach to the genre, here are the ten best Soulslikes with fluid movement mechanics.

Since I first played it, I think I've been one of Elden Ring Nightreign's most fervent critics, as it's a title that constantly contradicts me to the point of including it in a list of Soulslikes despite being developed by FromSoftware.

However, if there's one thing I not only can't complain about, but which I sincerely find masterful within the genre, it's the way it agilizes movement to a maximum. It gives each playthrough a dynamism uncommon in the genre.

Thanks to the characters' speed, their ability to climb walls, the spirit streams to jump to incredible heights, and the Spectral Hawk flight, which allows you to hover over areas with remarkable accuracy regarding your landing spot, simply wandering around is quite satisfying—a statement I can't make about almost any other title of this kind.

Is it cheating to include a game from the original influences' roots, which is also more of a roguelite, in this list? Perhaps, yet this is the first time the study has taken movement so seriously, so it deserves the mention.

Phantom Blade Zero is a fusion of traditional action-adventure elements with ideas borrowed from both Soulslikes and Metroidvanias, creating an extravagant yet highly satisfying cocktail.

The game boasts a staggering array of flashy weapons whose visual grandeur is breathtaking, especially in the hands of an ultra-powerful protagonist who is capable of putting those tools at the movement's mercy.

With the ability to sprint at high speed, swing on chains to cross gaps, run along walls, and use a grappling hook to reach high points, this title refuses to simply block doors on one side but instead strives to add depth to the exploration.

Unfortunately, most of these mechanics are prompts that can only be activated at specific, controlled locations, but they are more than enough to make Phantom Blade Zero a more dynamic game than average in this regard.

If you’re looking for the best FromSoftware-inspired ARPGs, I recommend the best Soulslikes based on critics' scores.

Speaking of middle ground, Nine Sols takes Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice's combat system and Hollow Knight's perspective, platforming, and exploration to create one of the decade's most wonderful indie games.

While it leans towards one or the other inspiration depending on the context, it's incredible how Yi soars across the maps once you've unlocked all of his movement tools, which are simple in concept but incredibly rewarding in execution.

Surely, it's nothing more than double jumps, dashes, and kicking enemies' skulls to get airborne, but it's enough to perfectly complement his prodigious combat mechanics.

Even if Nine Sols had terrible traversal, it would still be great because of how it shines in all the other elements, making the polished movement mechanics all the more admirable.

Especially considering it was released when Soulslikes were still in their infancy, Salt and Sanctuary was a major surprise, perfectly adapting the genre's formula to the 2D side-scrolling perspective.

With a wealth of secrets hidden behind the movement abilities you progressively unlock, it's a title that knows how to make platforming satisfying and imbue it with meaning beyond simply moving from point A to point B.

When you first change the gravity orientation, for example, you realize Salt and Sanctuary isn't just a great action RPG with challenging bosses and outstanding worldbuilding, but a game that understood that part of the Dark Souls trilogy's charm lay in how it transformed each new tool into a way to reinterpret the levels.

Years have passed, and I still believe it's the purest and most outstanding 2D Soulslike among those that don't venture too far into other genres, as few have captured the essence of their inspiration as well as this one.

Team Ninja is among the developers that have placed the most emphasis on the Soulslike genre, and while Rise of the Ronin isn't their most outstanding iteration, it certainly stands out when movement is the key factor.

Based on its open-world concept, the game boasts one of the most inventive arrays of traversal tools the genre has ever seen, offering a horse, a grappling hook, and a glider to facilitate the discovery of its expansive map.

If you compare it to direct peers like Ghost of Tsushima, it might fall short, but if the conversation turns to previous titles from the studio, such as Nioh, or games from FromSoftware, like the aforementioned Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, the tone shifts.

Ultimately, Rise of the Ronin combines a myriad of ideas that will appeal to some and deter others, though the fact that it brings with it a form of exploration that avoids relying solely on walking and fast travel is undeniable.

If you’re still waiting for the next FromSoftware game, check out these ten Soulslikes that most people haven’t played but definitely should.

Shattered - Tale of the Forgotten King is a fascinating title due to its attempt, although often erratic, to combine 3D combat with side-scrolling platforming, which is a unique approach even outside Soulslikes' spaces.

The combat is present and functional enough to sustain the experience for the hours it lasts, yet what truly catches the eye is the movement, as it feels like Journey thanks to its flow and smoothness.

In addition to its perspective shifts, which alternate between combat and 2.5D traversal, moving through its open world on a hoverboard feels compelling, mainly because of how unexpected it is to encounter such a mechanic in this type of game.

Indeed, there isn't much to do once you're in free-roaming areas, but since this article focuses on movement mechanics, Shattered - Tale of the Forgotten King keeps its place among the most distinguished in the genre.

While the first game in the series was pure action-adventure, and the second shifted towards open-world RPG elements, Darksiders 3 changed course once again, this time aiming to be both a Soulslike and a Metroidvania.

By merging the level design and combat system of the former with the progression and backtracking mechanics of the latter, Gunfire Games created a phenomenal symphony that truly draws on its hack-and-slash heritage.

Darksiders 3 embraces grandeur, allowing you to transform into diverse avatars to double jump and burn through barriers, glide on air currents, become an energy ball to cling to walls, or even walk on water.

If you add to all these different ways of traversing the use of Fury's whip to swing from platform to platform, the only logical conclusion left to draw is that Darksiders 3 is a marvel when it comes to moving around.

Another Crab's Treasure is among the most creatively designed Soulslikes we've had the pleasure of enjoying this decade, and its movement mechanics are anything but an exception.

The game's levels are extremely vertical and branching, so it needed movement methods that could handle its demanding platforming sections with jumps, climbs, glides, and directional grappling hooks that take you from one ledge to another in a matter of seconds.

It's no wonder the game has become a favorite among speedrunners; its open areas combined with its fluid maneuverability create the perfect breeding ground for exploring the limits of gravity and Krill's stamina.

It has incredible bosses, extensive customization, a remarkable audiovisual component, strong thematic cohesion... Another Crab's Treasure is a complete package, and thankfully, Aggro Crab didn't leave platforming out of the equation.

If you're looking for community-endorsed experiences, I recommend you try these ten Soulslikes where the user score is higher than the critic score.

After Hollow Knight established the Soulslite variant as an alternative for those who didn't want to fully commit to the formula, Hollow Knight: Silksong further solidified its fresh take on the genre.

The loss of resources upon death, save points that also serve as locations to modify your character, pattern-based bosses, cryptic lore... We all know the points of convergence, but where it truly breaks away is in its movement.

Even when compared to pure platformers, Hollow Knight: Silksong possesses a unique grace when it comes to traversal, with an incredibly agile Hornet who's capable of using her abilities in unique ways to facilitate her journey through Pharloom.

Grabbing ledges, bouncing off environmental elements, flying on air currents, leaping between walls, using your needle to propel yourself forward... The array of abilities available during the game is incredible and, above all, very satisfying, especially when you learn to chain them together and run without anything or anyone stopping you.

Nevertheless, beyond the games made by FromSoftware itself or titles that only tangentially touch on the genre, the purest example of a Soulslike with the most fluid movement mechanics is Valor Mortis.

Coming from Ghostrunner, One More Level leveraged its undeniable aptitude for first-person platforming and created an entire world around it, giving us an adventure where you jump, dash, swoop, and grapple with impressive ease.

Valor Mortis is already a striking project for its combination of such divergent concepts as stealth, first-person shooting, and ARPG combat based on parries, though adding such natural platforming sections on top of all that is simply incredible.

I spent the entire campaign amazed by the simple fact that Soulslikes don't move this fast and seamlessly, much less in sequences where you're speeding around in a minecart or running across platforms that are collapsing because a giant monster is attacking you with its tentacles.

Valor Mortis is a game that can be criticized for many things, but not for its movement. In fact, this is an area where it excels so much that other games should strive to emulate its talent.

From the indie ecosystem to productions approaching AAA measures, these are ten Soulslike franchises that should come back by 2027.

#4204. Marathon may actually have a shot as Server Slam hits it big on Steam

Marathon's latest public open weekend has kicked off, and it looks like enough people have showed up to play it.

Things are officially looking better for Marathon. The game’s Server Slam, essentially an open beta that’s freely available everywhere, has kicked off. This is the last chance for anyone curious about Bungie’s next big game to play it before it officially goes on sale next week.

Considering how unpopular the game has been throughout its development, and judging by the feedback from earlier closed beta tests, the turnout for the Server Slam is definitely encouraging.

The Marathon Server Slam has been online for a little over 12 hours on Steam, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. Only one of those platforms shares player numbers, of course, but it's enough to offer some visibility into how popular the test has been.

Immediately after servers went live, Marathon shot up the Steam most played charts. The game quickly achieved a peak of 143,621 concurrent players (via SteamDB), which is very respectable. Given that the Server Slam will be available for the entire weekend, there’s every chance the numbers will go up.

These figures are particularly encouraging when you look at Arc Raiders, the current top dog in the extraction shooter space, and the game that stole Marathon’s thunder last year when the two of them were being promoted by their publishers. Marathon, of course, got delayed out of 2025, which allowed Arc Raiders to launch first. It, of course, ended up proving that extraction shooters can be mainstream hits.

Like Marathon, Arc Raiders hosted its own server slam just a few days before its launch. That open test attracted 189,668 concurrent players at its peak, which is not that far off from Marathon’s so far.

Assuming positive word of mouth continues, more players are bound to jump in over the weekend and perhaps get Marathon to match or even exceed Arc Raiders’ record. At any rate, this is good news for beleaguered Bungie and points to what could be a big launch.

Marathon arrives March 5 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.

#4202. Interview: Goddess of Victory Nikke's dev team tell all about the hit shooter for its 4th anniversary

With Goddess of Victory: Nikke's fourth anniversary event just having taken place, the hit character-collecting shooter is riding high on its enduring popularity. This got us a bit curious about how things work behind the scenes with the folks at Shift Up.

So, we got the chance not only to put our questions to the dev team as a whole, but also to some specific members, such as graphics group lead Park Sanghu! Read on to find out more about what they had to say about this massive milestone year for Goddess of Victory: Nikke. General Dev Team Over the past four years, what have been the most exciting moments for Goddess of Victory: Nikke?

With NIKKE, we've always hoped to create events where mini-games, the 3D field, the story, the music, and the characters all come together and bring out the best in each other.

From that point of view, OVER ZONE was probably the most thrilling moment for us. It was the first time our vision for an event landed the way we hoped it would.

Honestly, if we could pick more than one, we would say every single anniversary event, because every anniversary and half-anniversary event has been a challenge for us, and each time the response from our Commanders has been gratifying.

We think there are so many games out there in the world, each offering something different to enjoy. NIKKE has a lot to offer too, but we would say the story has played the biggest part in its success.

We think a game's appeal depends on the timing being right. Fortunately, it seems the kind of experience we wanted to offer reached players at just the right time. In that sense, we've been genuinely lucky, and we're always grateful to our Commanders for the love they show to NIKKE.

Our design priorities vary depending on the Nikke's affiliation. For a manufacturer-affiliated Nikke, what matters is a design where the character's personality and concept come through at a glance—something that catches your interest and makes it easy to see the character's appeal.

Pilgrims, on the other hand, need to feel distinct from regular Nikkes. We want anyone who sees them to be left with a striking, flamboyant impression, so we focus on Nikke's signature original details and a high level of design intricacy, which give it a distinctive look.

Just as we previewed in the Developer's Note, and as demonstrated by some of the content showcased during the 4th Anniversary, we plan to continue building out features and systems that let players get even deeper into the story. We will share a more detailed roadmap in a future Developer's Note, so please stay tuned.

First of all, we are thrilled that we are now able to support Spanish in the game. Because we dedicate so much passion and effort to our story, We hope that Spanish language support brings enjoyment to even more of our Commanders.

Our hope is that even more fans will be able to enjoy wonderful experiences with NIKKE through offline events and expanded text language options in the future.We will do everything we can to help make that a reality. Park Sanghu (Graphics Group Lead) What makes Nikke's graphical style so distinct?

We would say Nikke's distinctive art style comes from the balance between three things: subtle rendering that brings out the full appeal of each character, a very high density of detail, and bold staging that ties it all together.

In particular, it's important to us to bring out each character's unique personality and silhouette while giving the same care to the finer details, from costumes and equipment to the texture of each material.

On top of that, we use lighting, colour, and composition to show each character at their best. We think that combination is what makes Nikke's art style so distinctive.

Our design priorities vary depending on the Nikke's affiliation. For a manufacturer-affiliated Nikke, what matters is a design where the character's personality and concept come through at a glance—something that catches your interest and makes it easy to see the character's appeal.

Pilgrims, on the other hand, need to feel distinct from regular Nikkes. We want anyone who sees them to be left with a striking, flamboyant impression, so we focus on Nikke's signature original details and a high level of design intricacy, which give it a distinctive look. Ju Jonghyeon a.k.a. Cosmograph (Sound Director) How did you approach the soundscape of Nikke? Stuff like the music, SFX and whatnot?

We believe that sound in games is more of a feedback element. That's why we always keep in mind what the top priority should be in each situation when working on the sound.

For interactions such as Character Touch SFX, our top priority is to bring out each character's charm. For Maria-n in the 4th Anniversary update, we wanted to further emphasise the musical contrast between different situations. We created a clear distinction between the music before and after meeting the Commander. By reducing the overall musical density, we aimed to bring each text-based action to life through sound.

We're always grateful to everyone who has continued to trust us and wait patiently.We will do our utmost to deliver a better game and an improved service.

Now that what could be considered Part 1 of the story has largely unfolded, we believe we can offer players a fresher and more exciting experience in Part 2. Please continue to support us going forward, and we wish you all good health Some pretty interesting tidbits about what Nikke's development process is like, and a couple of hints about the future! While Nikke has had a rocky month with their recent PC launcher troubles, it seems that was only a bit of a stumble. So hopefully, in the future we'll see Goddess of Victory: Nikke once more going from strength to strength.

Of course, to do that they'll also have to cope with some other up-and-coming competitors. You can check out some of the biggest hits of the past year making waves on smartphones with our list of the best mobile games of 2026 (so far)!

#4201. The Sims 4 is getting paid mods, and a new in-game currency to pay for them

The Sims 4 is about to launch a couple of major initiatives that may not exactly be what players have been looking for.

The Sims 4 has officially entered into its paid mods era. Developer Maxis announced The Sims Maker Program, and The Sims 4 Marketplace - two new destinations to publish, and discover new add-on content.

The two new features will arrive first on PC and Mac, starting March 17. PlayStation and Xbox players will receive them over the next couple of months, which is very much in line with how other franchises have rolled out their own paid mods systems.

The Maker Program is a way for community creators to get their work out there, and profit from it. The content they create will end up on the Marketplace, where other players can browse it, and pay for it if they want to use it in their game.

Created content will be available across all platforms. All previous packs The Sims 4 players should be familiar with will move to the Marketplace, too: once the feature launches, this is where you’re going to find Expansion Packs, Game Packs, Stuff Packs, Kits, and other official additions created by Maxis.

Alongside this, the game is also introducing a new virtual currency - Moola - which is what you’re going to use to purchase Maker Packs, as well as Sims 4 Kits in the Marketplace. A portion of your purchase will go to the creator (roughly 30%) of what you buy.

It is worth noting, however, that you’ll still be able to buy Expansion Packs, Game Packs, and Stuff Packs without having to purchase Moola, or go through the Marketplace. Kits are the only items that will no longer be available on the existing PC/console storefronts. Moola comes in the usual denominations you’ve seen a hundred items in other games’ in-game shops.

In order to start creating custom content and publishing it on the Marketplace, you’ll need to first be accepted into the program. Once that’s done, you’ll be able to directly publish your content on the Marketplace.

In the blog post announcing the new features, Maxis said that creators will have control over the price of their content, and how it's packaged. These are referred to as Maker Packs, which can include Create-a-Sim or Build/Buy items.

You can apply to become a Maker from March 5. Once accepted, you’ll also get access to the Maker Suite, which is what you’re going to use to test your work to ensure it runs smoothly on the different platforms, and eventually publish it.

#4200. Warhammer Survivors review - "It's got the heart, but not the spark."

Back before Vampire Survivors hit iOS and Android, there were already a number of games inspired by (or, some might say, ripping off) their formula. So much so that I was wondering if it would go the way of Fall Guys/Stumble Guys, and be outshined by others who had gotten to mobile first.

But while those other games still have their fans, Poncle’s arrival on mobile only increased the popularity of Vampire Survivors. So much so that Auroch Digital reached out to create their own spinoff, dubbed Warhammer Survivors, that seeks to do for roguelites what Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun did for boomer shooters!

So, now Warhammer Survivors is out in the wild. But does it hold up to the indie hit that is Vampire Survivors? Hammer time If you’ve played Vampire Survivors, then you know what to expect from Warhammer Survivors. And to their credit, Auroch Digital maintain much of the same gameplay loop and fun of dealing with hordes of enemies, albeit with some interesting twists on the formula, such as different mechanics for each faction, like toxic debuffs from Nurgle or a hive-mind aspect for Tyranids.

For fans of AoS and 40,000, it's a robust offering, as Warhammer Survivors splits each universe into its own sub-game with its own progression. That means different levels, enemies and weapons, although many of them will feel somewhat similar in everything but looks.

If you’re a Vampire Survivors fan, this’ll all seem quite familiar, but Warhammer Survivors can also feel a lot more difficult due to the slower-paced movement of your character and the more dangerous enemies. Depending on your perspective, that’s either a good or a bad thing, but it definitely makes you feel as if there’s more at stake when you get cornered.

And while the weapons and gadgets feel familiar to what we've seen before, there are enough tweaks to make them feel different. One particularly interesting mechanic is that when you pick up a weapon your character is incompatible with, another character joins your party. While mostly cosmetic, their positioning affects where their attacks spring from, and if nothing else, it makes you feel as if you’re leading your own Kill Team into battle. Reference Overloaded Probably the most Warhammer thing about it is the number of references and nods to the original franchise. Whether that’s collecting paint pots to unlock new characters, all the iconic weapons, or even power-ups inspired by various gubbins from the hobby (blast templates, my beloved).

Basically, if you’ve ever been a fan of Warhammer 40,000 or Age of Sigmar, you’ll enjoy the nods to the hobby’s lengthy history. But if you’re a newcomer who, for whatever reason, has picked this up as your first Warhammer experience, you’ll be left feeling somewhat confused.

Imperium Sound (& Graphics) System One aspect where Warhammer Survivors is thrashed by the original Vampire Survivors is in its soundtrack and SFX. The bit-crushed music and impact of weapons don’t match up to the original, and feel more than a little flat at times. I was excited to hear about the 80s/90s rock and electronic mashup music, but nothing really hits the same way that tracks such as Mad Forest, Moms are Tough, or Gatti Amari do when you’re really in the zone.

The graphics, however, are perfectly acceptable, albeit without the same amount of charm as Vampire Survivors. But you’ll find all your favourite Warhammer characters crushed up into some tasty bits that make them instantly recognisable, but also feel distinctly Survivors-like, and the colourful locations manage to feel authentically grimdark while contrasting one another.

Oi- we’re the bloody Ubersreik five! Now, there is one big omission here, and, of course, it’s the setting of The Old World. Not to sound like a grognard, but while Age of Sigmar is a perfectly worthy setting to draw from, Warhammer Fantasy, which kicked off the entire IP, has roared back into popularity in recent years. We get Gotrek Gurnisson, undoubtedly one of the most recognisable characters from The Old World, but no other nods to the original grimdark fantasy universe.

It’s a shame, because what’s already here is a great love letter to Warhammer. Hopefully, we’ll see some updates down the line, and heck, I’d even take a paid DLC to see content inspired by Warhammer Fantasy make an appearance. With more updates down the line, this could be the case, and there’re plenty of spinoffs in Games Workshop’s wider line that’d make for excellent one-off levels or characters to join the battle. So here’s hoping Auroch take advantage of the vast depth of the IP. Grindhammer I actually put off publishing this review because I wanted to put more time into Warhammer Survivors. And I did, to the tune of around three or so hours, which isn’t much in the grand scheme of things but usually more than enough to get a feel for a game; especially a fast-paced roguelite. Yet, I couldn’t help but feel I was missing something that might really change how I felt about it. But every time I played, it felt like I was making only the most incremental progress, even though (as you'll find) I was chugging along at a quite even pace.

And to me, that’s my main issue with Warhammer Survivors. Whereas Vampire Survivors feels like it moves fast, with you quickly unlocking new stages, weapons and abilities, Warhammer Survivors is much slower in terms of progression. Add to that the fact that you have two separate universes with (mostly) completely different progression, and what should be exciting, rapid progress quickly becomes a slog.

Although it’s been a while, I feel as if in five hours of Vampire Survivors I was already headed towards that 30-minute mark, exploring multiple levels and already well on my way to experiencing new weapon fusions and upgrades. Maybe it’s me getting older, or it’s that Warhammer Survivors simply feels smaller and less engaging than its spiritual predecessor, especially considering that even though I felt I was making slow progress, it seems I've already completed 14% of the 40k side of the equation!

A lot of the issues with progression and how slow it seems, I feel, are that aforementioned difficulty. Now, there’s a joke about game journalists and difficulty there, but let me explain. In Vampire Survivors, you’re encouraged to move, to explore the map and dodge enemies, thereby encountering more secrets and upgrades. Meanwhile, Warhammer Survivors’ more punishing damage encourages you to hunker down, and only move if you see an existing secret highlighted on the map.

That means that, while you play for the same amount of time, you feel as if you’ve found less (even if you've actually found more). And yes, it’s perfectly fun watching hordes of Tyranids fall to your bolters and las-rifle fire, but it’s not quite as exciting as whipping your way through hordes of bats. While it may be more Warhammer to pick a spot and stick to it as you fortify your position, it sort of misses the point of a fast-paced bullet heaven.

Point being, I love Warhammer, I love Vampire Survivors; so this should have me in a chokehold. But it simply doesn’t. It feels like a perfectly fine love letter to the franchise, yet it never quite hits the heights that Vampire Survivors did. And while it may feel unfair for me to continuously compare the two, it’s hard not to when Survivors is in the title.

Maybe, with the coming updates Auroch have promised, it’ll be able to stand on its own two feet. Even so, I can heartily recommend it if you’re either a Warhammer fan, or you’ve completely rinsed everything Vampire Survivors has to offer. Just be aware that recommendation comes with a few asterisks.

#4198. Our first look at Diablo 4's Warlock and the game's next season arrive in today's livestream - watch it here

Diablo 4's latest Developer Update is nearly upon us, and it's one plenty of the game's fans and players have been looking forward to.

Diablo 4’s next, long-awaited Developer Update finally airs today. This meaty livestream was first announced nearly a month ago, when Blizzard initially revealed that the game’s next class is the Warlock.

The Warlock’s initial unveiling, however, was incredibly brief, showing no gameplay. It also didn't explain how the class is going to fit within the existing roster. This all changes today.

The Warlock is one of two classes coming to Diablo 4 with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion. The first, the Paladin, is already available in the game for anyone who pre-orders the expansion. The Warlock will instead arrive alongside the expansion on April 28.

Among the topics the Developer Update will cover are the Killstreaks system, as well as Bloodstained items. As always, you can also expect a Q&A segment at the end of the show, and I imagine there’s going to be a few about the Warlock.

#4197. Diablo 4's next season is short, but it lets you become The Butcher, and it has Doom: The Dark Ages skins you probably can't afford

Blizzard has unveiled the next Diablo 4 season, which kicks off next week to hold us over until the launch of the game's big expansion in April.

The big Diablo 4 Developer Update has indeed delivered the goods. One of the livestream’s big topics was, of course, the game’s upcoming mini-season, which is set to kick off next week and run until the launch of Lord of Hatred, the game’s anticipated next expansion.

You can tell Blizzard wanted to have a bit of fun with Season of Slaughter, as many of its major features make it look like a limited-time event, but there is plenty to be excited about here.

Season of Slaughter kicks off March 11, and will run until the following season kicks off April 28, with the launch of the Lord of Hatred expansion. Many of the season’s biggest additions were available to preview in the 2.6.0 Public Test Realm.

Patch 2.6.0, as you might have guessed, is the one that will kick off the slaughter next week. The headline feature here is ability to become The Butcher, the iconic in-game boss who randomly invades players’ games.

When you play as The Butcher, you’ll be rewarded the more kills you get in quick succession. Your skills hotbar will transform to become something more fitting of The Butcher, making them more brutal. You’ll also earn a seasonal currency as you play.

Starting the seasonal questline is how you can begin to assume The Butcher’s form. A Taste of Power can be initiated from Gea Kul. Transforming into The Butcher can be done in a few ways. As you play, you’ll earn Meaty Offerings, which can later be spent on Shrines of Slaughter in the new Helltide. Once activated, the shrine will draw more enemies towards you.

If you never venture into PvP zones in Diablo 4, this season may change your mind. The standard PvP combat that could only be found in Fields of Hatred has been replaced with a Ceremony of Slaughter, a new event that rewards you for killing enemies quickly. See it through and The Butcher’s Idol will spawn, allowing you to transform into it.

Elsewhere in the world, you’ll also be able to attain the same power at Slaughterhouses, a new activity type available this season. Inside, you immediately become The Butcher for the entirety of the run.

The Butcher’s arrival also ties into two of the other Season of Slaughter’s more interesting additions. First, the Killstreak system finally arrives in Diablo 4, rewarding you for being as efficient as possible in carving your way through enemies.

Anyone who played Diablo 3 should be familiar with how it works. It kicks off the moment you get a kill, and has a visible timer where you’ll need continue performing the same action to up your streak. The more kills you get, the more often your timer will refresh.

There are five tiers to climb through: Killstreak, Carnage, Devastation, Bloodbath, and Massacre. You’re awarded for the tier you manage to reach before the timer runs out. You’ll earn XP and seasonal rep each time a Killstreak is achieved.

The other Butcher-themed addition is Bloodied Items, which is a new item quality available throughout this season. They play into the Killstreak system to grant you even more power. Bloodied Items come with unique affixes that scale off your Killstreak tier. You’ll see many familiar items in that pool, as any item in the game has a chance to drop as Bloodied. Bloodied Items can also be acquired by earning Fresh Meat.

Even if none of that sounds exciting, you’re probably going to redownload the game for The Paladin free trial, which kicks off alongside the new season on March 11. The trial is only available until March 18, and it lets you try out the Paladin class.

The trial is available across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. You’ll be able to take the new class for a spin, but your progress will be capped at level 25. The Paladin can be permanently unlocked by buying the Lord of Hatred expansion, as it’s one of two classes the expansion is introducing.

The good news is that any progress you make in the free trial will carry over to the full game if/when you buy the expansion.

Season of Slaughter also kicks off a Doom: The Dark Ages collaboration event. As we’ve come to expect, there’s a very limited free component to the collaboration, in the form of the Doom Reliquary. This is essentially a mini-battle pass that includes the Shield Saw skin, Slayer’s Flair, the head of the Cyberdemon as a back trophy and various other smaller bits.

The more impressive items - such as character skins, will instead be available to purchase for real money. The list includes the Doom Slayer armor, Mecha Dragon Serrat skin for your cat mount, and a Cacodemon pet.

Though the armor skin is cross-class compatible, judging by how much previous collaboration items have cost in Diablo 4, most of us probably won’t be spending that kind of money to get it.

#4196. Petit Planet Hands-On Preview – Creature Comforts

Petit Planet marks Hoyoverse’s maiden voyage into the life sim genre popularized by games like Animal Crossing, Stardew Valley, and, most recently, Pokémon Pokopia. The creators of Genshin Impact, Honkai: Star Rail, and Zenless Zone Zero have crafted well-received, lucrative free-to-play gacha games across several disparate genres; Petit Planet, fittingly, sees it try to attract yet another world of players. It’s been a year since I first played Petit Planet’s initial alpha test, and I spent a couple of more hours exploring its cozy cosmos at the Hoyoverse Media Tour in Seoul, South Korea. Although what I played has not dramatically changed my opinion of the game – it remains a delightful, if familiar, good time – speaking to its lead designer who goes by the single name Murphy and lead artist Yunli Huang helped shed light on how Petit Planet will differentiate itself from contemporaries and its approach to multiplayer, storytelling, and monetization.

The game’s premise centers on a customizable protagonist who sets out to populate their own personal planet (which is about the size of King Kai’s world from Dragon Ball Z). Although you are ostensibly human, everyone else is a talking animal. Your mentor of sorts is a chillax sheepdog named Mobai, who enjoys wearing straw hats and dropping his catchphrase/life mantra “Mo worries” and “Mo Rush.” The business-minded Glenn the Squirrel is a shopkeeper and seems like a cuter, less aggressive Tom Nook. Yunghou is a shy fox who enjoys farming and has the slightest hint of a southern accent. These critters and many more inhabit your planet, which you’ll grow from an empty (but vibrant) rock into a bustling village filled with homes, businesses, crops, decor, and, of course, neighbors.

Story is rarely a hook for a genre that largely promotes creating your own fun through the emergent moments with your neighbors and friends in multiplayer. Still, after Pokémon Pokopia presented an unexpectedly wild and fascinating tale, I ask if players should bother getting invested in a grander narrative à la Genshin Impact. The short answer seems to be “not so much.”

“Unlike other Hoyoverse games, there is no such main plot,” Murphy explains in my group interview. “There will be a main story at the beginning, but the main purpose is just to guide the players, get more familiar with the setting and the world. But the whole narrative of this game will be more fragmented. For example, if you look at those descriptions of those items, there will be a lot of content and narrative behind it. If you look at the description of creatures, many of them are real creatures in real world, and you get to learn more knowledge of this creature by reading those descriptions. And also, we've developed a very comprehensive narrative for each of our neighbors, so that is also part of our, called like, main plot, main narrative, because we want to make this world more like more lively and a more livable world. So that is how we treat narrative in this game."

While players who enjoy a substantial story to propel them through a game may be disappointed, those looking to unwind with a laid-back experience should be pleased. Hoyoverse is designing Petit Planet to be a no-pressure experience to enjoy at your leisure, hence why it emphasizes it as a life sim more than a management sim. There are no complicated stats to manage; simple inputs make it easy to pick up and play; imperfection is encouraged, with Hoyoverse comparing the experience to doodling as a child: your creation may not be perfect, but you had fun bringing your imagination to life.

I spent the first hour of my roughly two-and-a-half-hour session starting from scratch to see if any notable changes were made to this introductory portion in the last year. If there are any differences, they’re imperceptible because I wen went through the same onboarding of learning how to catch bugs and fish, building your first home, inviting your first neighbor, and farming crops, all while growing a magical sapling that, after performing enough tasks, blooms into a full tree that brings new life and mechanics to your world as it grows. Performing special tasks for residents, from completing requests to simply interacting with them, grows their bond, which, when high enough, will entice them to move in. For veteran genre fans, it’s a familiar song and dance. What I did notice this time around is how refreshingly quick the onboarding is. You have all of these foundational mechanics within the first 45 to 50 minutes, which is a nice pace. It was a good refresher for some foundational mechanics I’d forgotten since I last played, but it created an appetite to dive deeper.

Thankfully, Hoyoverse provided a second build set many hours into the game to give an idea of how planets can evolve. This build was set during winter, one of Petit Planet’s revolving seasons that alter the environment and introduce themed cosmetics and decor for players and residents. Sporting winter gear, I ran around the snow-covered planet, which was densely populated with shops, homes, and neighbors. I was initially greeted by unfamiliar faces named Trixie and Kookoo, who provided weather forecasts and news reports reminiscent of Isabelle from Animal Crossing and Callie and Marie from Splatoon. My sparse quest log was tricky to tackle since they revolved around mechanics I had no context for, such as setting up Vignettes. These are essentially templates for unique scenes filled out by dropping the correct furniture pieces in their layout; in this case, I had to set up an outdoor movie on the beach.

I only spent roughly an hour with this late build, and my biggest takeaway was simply how dense and lovely the village looked. A lot of work went into crafting this build, which boasted a farm filled with different crops (with unlockable recipes to create dishes from them), crafting tables to build furniture from collectible blueprints, and several shops, including Glenn’s to purchase a revolving selection of decor items. None of what I saw surprised me, however. Petit Planet so far checks many of the boxes you’d expect and want from a life sim. My cursory tour of a later-game planet did little to reveal any big new ideas, but what I did experience seemed perfectly cromulent.

My biggest question regards multiplayer. As much as I enjoy Animal Crossing: New Horizons and Pokémon Pokopia as solo experiences, playing with friends feels like a mean joke because of the tedious number of hoops to jump through just to invite other players into your world. And even once your buddy arrives, interactions are disappointingly limited. When I ask if Petit Planet offers a comparatively frictionless multiplayer experience, Murphy vaguely assures smoother sailing. “The multiplayer experience is a very important part of our game because, just as the interaction with NPCs, the interaction with other players is also a form of building up emotional connection to this game, and we want to provide that kind of experience to our players.” More specifically, Murphy cites features such as dynamic server load adjustments based on player counts and the option to allow or ban visiting players from taking resources from your planet to prevent griefing.

As a free-to-play Hoyoverse game, monetization is a major talking point. In Petit Planet’s case, the team agrees that rolling for neighbors gacha-style would be strange and defeats the spirit of the genre. Instead, all monetization will revolve around cosmetics; players can unlock new furniture and themed decor sets, outfits, and other cosmetic accessories for their character. Unlocking a full themed set of decor earns currency points, and there are myriad reward meters to fill for performing mundane tasks like greeting residents or catching bugs. It remains to be seen if and how Petit Planet’s progression begins nudging players into opening their wallets, but Hoyoverse promises it will be an experience that deemphasizes grinding.

I also briefly checked out the recently announced Switch 2 version of Petit Planet. My impressions after about 15 minutes of playtime: it’s fine. It sometimes ran noticeably hitchier than the PC version I spent most of my time with, but it seems perfectly adequate so far and, hopefully, will be a smooth experience when it launches sometime next year.

Since life sims require more than a couple of hours to fully reveal their quality, it was tough to get a read on Petit Planet even with this new showing. The game looks beautiful thanks to Hoyoverse’s signature sharp and colorful visual style. It has a relaxing vibe, and feels mechanically decent for the most part. In short, it seems broadly fine and like a respectable take on the genre. I suspect its biggest appeal will be that it will receive what Animal Crossing: New Horizons lacked: years of constant, substantial support.

Hoyoverse is very good about keeping fans of its games well fed with regular updates for years on end, and I don’t expect it to stop now. The idea of a seemingly well-made spin on Animal Crossing that’s free to download and, unless it completely bombs, will almost certainly receive years of new content is enticing on paper. I imagine this is the reason Petit Planet is coming to Switch 2 next year, where it can lure in Animal Crossing and Pokopia players before other consoles. PC and mobile players, meanwhile, must only wait until December 4 when Petit Planet fully launches to see if it has the chops to stand alongside the coziest giants of the genre.
