#4195. The Wrapp - Warhammer Survivors, chickens crossing colourful roads, and feline Sudoku

Hello! And welcome back to The Wrapp. This time, a bunch of the team have been swept up in Warhammer fever, though they disagree on its quality. Elsewhere, Dann is ticking along with his usual smorgasbord of games while Shaun is losing sleep counting cats. Apparently, they're less therapeutic than sheep. I assume because they look less like fluffy clouds.

Warhammer Survivors… Need I say more? Okay, I'll say a bit more. Leading up to its release, Warhammer Survivors touted that it was going to be just that: Vampire Survivors with Warhammer theming, visuals, and a couple of tweaked mechanics. And it has succeeded very well. It is perhaps one of the greatest waiting games released since Angry Birds, and I'm looking forward to exploring more of it and any DLC that comes with it.

And to those certain reviews that have criticised it for not blowing their minds… What were you expecting? We were all told that we were gonna get a duck and we got a duck. If you downloaded and played expecting a goose, my friend, that's on you.

Unfortunately, I have succumbed to peer pressure (and by that, I mean Will and Iwan) and have downloaded Warhammer Survivors on my phone. I lasted a full minute before I inevitably died on my first go. I wish I could say that a fearsome boss took me down in a blaze of glory after my valiant efforts of trying to overcome it, but in reality, a swarm of rats rushed towards me, I got caught in the stampede, and I promptly perished.

So I guess that means I need to spend the entirety of my weekend trying to take vengeance on those rats. Look out, rodents, here I come!

This week is Into the Wild for Pokémon Go, and so I’ll be spending a large portion of my weekend walking around with fellow trainers, trying to nab shinies and hundos. Outside of that, I’m continuing my search for the perfect run in 80 Days (my most recent run ended with me freezing to death near the North Pole) and keeping chipping away at MH: Outlanders.

I’ll be honest, after playing so much mobile this week, I may be taking a break. I’ve put a lot of time into Warhammer Survivors and, while I’ve been enjoying it, it hasn’t quite clicked with me the way that Vampire Survivors did. Read my whole Warhammer Survivors review for the breakdown, but as many people have opined, it feels a bit like what it is: a simple spinoff that lacks the meat of the original.

That being said, I will be putting more time into it since I’m in a bit of a Warhammer mood. However, Titanium Court is still begging for my attention too. Either way, I’ll be sure to try and put a bit of time into something over the weekend since, well, it’s my job after all. And lord knows I can’t wait to get my hands on Gotrek in Warhammer Survivors!

Being as I am a man of increasing age, my days of gaming until the small hours are behind me, or so I thought. It was but Wednesday night, however, when I found myself accidentally up until 1 am, so enthralled was I by this latest game I found. Was it Ocarina of Time, was it a Grand Theft Auto? No, it was Mewodoku.

For those not in the meknow - see, I can do it too, just not as well - it is the age-old game of Sudoku with cat faces. That's a very reductive description, cause theres also one cat per colour with lines going all over the place. Whatever it is, I am smitten. The puzzles get genuinely challenging, the music is so calming, and I am currently at the top of the leaderboard! It is probably all bots or children, but I will happily stand on top of little Timmy at the summit of Meowdoku.

As you'll know from reading this Wrapp, one game has taken our virtual office by storm. Slaying hordes of enemies in Warhammer Survivors seems to be the order of the day. As such, I've got no choice but to try Crossy Road Rush. That's right. With all the grittiness and gore flying about right now, I fancy a palate cleanser. So I'll dive into the colourful world of endless running for an hour or two. Once its sugary goodness makes me feel a little sick, maybe then I'll pivot to chunky pixel violence.

#4193. PlayStation Adds Major Feature to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, ARC Raiders, and More

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

A big component of what makes the PS5 an attractive console, besides just being able to play particular games you can’t play elsewhere, is the console’s various built-in graphical perks. Since the PS5 first launched in 2020, its hardware power has remained one of its definitive perks, with the PS5 Pro in particular taking matters further with the inclusion of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution, better known as PSSR.

In this list, we discuss some of the best PS4 games to play with the PS5 Pro's Image Quality Enhancements option.

Even though the PS5 already has a few years under its belt, the brand isn’t just resting on its proverbial laurels and letting its existing hardware carry it. New advancements in graphical technology are coming out all the time, and even games that looked pretty stunning when they first dropped like Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 can always look a little bit better.

To that end, PlayStation has added support for one of its up-and-coming graphical frameworks, Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), to several more games in the PS5’s library following its initial launch last month exclusively in Marvel’s Wolverine and Ghost of Yotei. The newly-upscaled games include Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, Control Resonant, ARC Raiders, The Finals, No Man’s Sky, and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam.

In case you forgot, QSSR is a proprietary AI upscaling framework created in tandem between PlayStation and AMD. This framework came about from Project Amethyst, an ongoing developmental effort between both companies that also gave rise to PSSR. According to the official announcement of the newly-upscaled games on the official PlayStation news blog, QSSR provides “sharper details, cleaner edges, and more stable images than traditional upscalers,” and since it’s built on the same platform as PSSR, it’s easy for games that already use that framework to incorporate it.

QSSR is a proprietary AI upscaling framework created in tandem between PlayStation and AMD.

In that news post, PlayStation got quotes from all of the improved games’ developers on how QSSR has affected their respective titles. Insomniac Games’ Mike Fitzgerald said that, after incorporating the tech into the launch of Marvel’s Wolverine, the studio decided to go back and add it to Marvel’s Spider-Man 2 as well. “We’re excited for players to swing back into our 2023 title and see QSSR’s exciting image stability and sharpness benefits in both Fidelity and Performance modes,” he said.

Sony has introduced a brand-new AI-powered upscaling technology called Quick Spectral Super Resolution.

Remedy Entertainment’s Erik Jansson said that “QSSR gives Control Resonant a much more stable and detailed image, and we’ve worked closely with Sony to have it ready in an update coming in December.”

Embark Studios’ Mikael Linderholm said that QSSR support will be coming soon to ARC Raiders and The Finals, and said that his studio is “very happy to see Sony’s continued investment in PlayStation technology translate into meaningful improvements for all players.”

While I’m personally of the belief that graphics alone don’t automatically make a game good, it is still pretty interesting to see the degree to which graphical fidelity can be improved, especially as we start to run up against the proverbial limits of realism.

Obviously, the use of AI in games is a feisty topic, particularly in presentation elements like voice acting. In the specific use case of graphics, some efforts like NVIDIA’s AI-powered DLSS5 and its widely-mocked “yassify filter” on character models is probably not the optimal way to be going about this. Rather than trying to generate and overwrite existing graphics with slop, something like QSSR is closer to the ideal, taking what’s already present and merely smoothing out the rougher edges of the environmental rendering process.

PlayStation has promised that this tech will be coming to more games, ending its news post by saying, “Developers are just getting started, and we’re excited to keep working with them to bring QSSR to more games on PS5 in the coming months.”

Two classic apocalyptic shooters have received free modern graphical facelifts.

#4192. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.

#4191. Warhammer Survivors reveals its roadmap, with new characters, weapons and cross-save on the way

One of my colleagues gave Warhammer Survivors a go this week and lasted about a minute before a stampede of rats ran them over. The weekend has since been set aside for revenge. Good timing, because Auroch Digital has just revealed a roadmap for the Survivors-like, which is out now on iOS and Android, and there’s a lot more on the way to die to.

Most of the roadmap includes free updates over the next few months, adding new characters and weapons to both the Warhammer 40,000 and Age of Sigmar halves, along with QoL fixes. Smaller patches will fill the gaps between the bigger drops, with some of them landing before the end of the year.

Cross-save is coming as well, and since it launched on just about everything at once (phones, Switch, PlayStation, Xbox and PC), being able to carry a run’s worth of unlocks from the sofa to the tube is the update I’d look forward to most. The bigger piece of content is still under wraps, listed only as [REDACTED], with a few clues tucked into the roadmap image for anyone who fancies some detective work.

Our Warhammer Survivors review is live now too, and Iwan’s verdict is that it’s got the heart, but not the spark. The office hasn’t agreed on it either, as this week’s Wrapp makes fairly clear. The thing is, Vampire Survivors didn’t arrive fully formed.

A lot of what people love about it came in over years of updates and expansions, and the version on your phone now is a very different beast from the one that first went viral. Heart’s the harder thing to patch in. If Auroch keeps this pace, I’d back the spark to show up sooner rather than later.

Warhammer Survivors is out now on the App Store and Google Play.

And if the rats keep winning, our list of this week’s new mobile games is somewhere else to spend the weekend.

#4190. Nintendo May Have Just Teased a Beloved Zelda Game Coming to Switch Online

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

It's been a little over a week since the release of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, but Zelda fans are already hungry for more (and I include myself there!).

And while Nintendo hasn't announced another major release for the franchise just yet, a curious discovery on the company's official website has sparked speculation that one beloved adventure could finally be making its way to Nintendo Switch Online.

Following the remake’s launch, Nintendo recently launched a new section on Nintendo.com dedicated to the full catalog of games in The Legend of Zelda franchise.

Called “Game History”, the page lists the series' entries in release order, allowing visitors to explore the history of Hyrule and see which platforms each adventure originally launched on. You can also sort and filter the games however you like, and there's even a lovely little feature that shows how old you were when each Zelda game came out!

Nintendo has announced that the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time became the fastest selling Switch 2 game in under a week.

However, the most interesting detail is that Nintendo's website also indicates which games are playable through Nintendo Switch Online. And that's where things get a little strange.

As spotted by fans on Reddit, The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds is currently listed as playable with Nintendo Switch Online on the official website. That's particularly interesting because the 2013 adventure was originally released for the Nintendo 3DS and isn't currently available through the subscription service.

As spotted by fans on Reddit, The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds is currently listed as playable with Nintendo Switch Online on the official website.

Naturally, this has led some players to believe Nintendo might be preparing to bring the beloved handheld classic to modern platforms and just let that accidentally slip! But I gotta say, A Link Between Worlds is widely regarded as one of the standout entries in the franchise, and its unique mechanic of allowing Link to transform into a painting and move along walls would definitely make for a welcome addition to the Switch Online library.

The first gameplay trailer for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has confirmed that it has added a beloved feature from the 3DS version.

Still, not everyone is convinced this is an intentional tease. Some players believe the listing is simply a website error that Nintendo will eventually correct – after all, the company hasn't announced any plans to introduce Nintendo 3DS games to Switch Online, and the service doesn't currently offer a dedicated 3DS game library.

It is important to highlight that, at the time of writing, Nintendo hasn't publicly addressed the listing or announced that A Link Between Worlds is coming to Nintendo Switch Online. And the game is still marked as playable through the service on the official website, but that alone isn't enough to confirm anything!

Of course, this wouldn't be the first time Nintendo fans have found themselves digging through official websites for clues about upcoming releases. And considering how many classic Zelda adventures remain unavailable on modern hardware, it's easy to understand why this particular discovery has generated excitement.

For now, I'd recommend keeping expectations in check! A Link Between Worlds joining Nintendo Switch Online would be fantastic news, but until Nintendo says something officially, this is still firmly in rumor territory. Hopefully, it's a mistake that the company won't be correcting anytime soon.

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

#4189. Talking Point: What's Your Favourite Tiny Tweak In Zelda: Ocarina Of Time?

While the Ocarina of Time we see on Switch 2 is undoubtedly the same game we all know from the N64, there are enough tweaks in there that have had the biggest fans amongst us clicking and pointing at the screen like that Leonardo DiCaprio meme.

We're not talking about the big changes, either. You can keep your new visuals, fancy jump buttons and modern camera controls; we're getting excited over new floor textures and wall decals — stuff that wouldn't stand out unless you had played the original more times than you care to admit.

Below, we have shared our favourite tiny tweaks that have stood out so far. Some are more niche than others, but these are the little changes that had us beaming in our first few hours of rediscovering Hyrule and finding it not quite as we remember it.

After you've read through our picks, why not head to the comments and share your top tweaks?

Editor's Note. If there's any Zelda-related topic (or, indeed, anything else game-related) you'd like to bring to the attention of NL and the community, remember you can also submit letters for our monthly letters page. The mailbox is looking per-ritty empty at the time of writing, and we'd wager it's down to a certain November game keeping you all occupied!

Knowing the original game like the back of my hand, I'm yet to walk into a room without going, "Oooh, look how they changed that bit!" But the one that has stood out to me the most so far is being able to ride Epona right up to the entrance to Kakariko Village without getting chucked off at the bottom of the stairs.

Does it change the game in any way at all? Absolutely not. But praise be to whichever innovative dev at Nintendo thought, 'What if Jim didn't have to sit through a backtracking animation every time he forgot to dismount quickly enough?'

The ragdoll may not be a substantial inclusion, but if I can pick between a stiff, canned animation of Link collapsing to the floor and seeing his lifeless body tumble into the rapids that lead up to Zora's Domain, you know what I'm going to choose.

The option to remove one of the few tweaks I haven’t enjoyed so far — Navi’s incessant dialogue boxes commenting on everything — is a godsend. I was concerned she’d spend the entire game puncturing the mood with “Oooh, big mountain!” and “Wow, great work!” and “OMG, that was a lucky escape!” (I’m paraphrasing, but that’s the gist), and she does.

Turning on the ‘Master’ display option, though, reduces the UI to the bare minimum, removing almost everything, including Navi’s dialogue boxes. So when I emerge onto Hyrule Field, the landscape speaks for itself (with a little help from the music). Bliss. Other people might enjoy her interjections, and yes, I will miss a cute line or two, but thanks for letting me turn off the running commentary, Nintendo.

Turning Grouch Mode off, the slingshot easter egg in the courtyard window is ace. And Kakariko feels more like a real place now. And those little rivulets on Hyrule Field add so much. And that part of Lon Lon... *babbling trails off...

Without heading into spoiler territory, I suppose my niche tweak (if it’s considered niche) would be the addition of Threads of Time, but more specifically the Tapestry.

I’ve filled out my tapestry now, but throughout each stage of Link’s journey it was nice to see the progress I was making. I jumped into the remake with the hope of experiencing it with fresh eyes (although I’d played the original), and it really felt like it at times. It was also a really good way for me to gauge what I could do next should I forget, collectables I likely still needed, or even secrets I still had to unlock.

It’s a very simple addition common in modern gaming, but a tweak which was needed.

I’m enjoying all the revamped music, but one arrangement that took me by surprise is when you encounter common or garden foes. There’s more urgency and danger now: notes are sharply cutting in, there’s a subtle, unnerving rise and fall in volume, and if the battle lasts long enough, it goes up a notch when a horn (I’m guessing!) is eventually layered on top.

For a track I hadn’t given a second’s thought to in the original, I’m now delighted every time an enemy nears.

Note. Very minor pre-Hyrule Field spoilers ahead...

Some of the subtle tweaks to Ocarina of Time’s narrative landed so well with me. I won’t go into the later examples, but I absolutely adored the moment when Link runs into both Mido and Saria after leaving the Deku Tree.

Mido, who feels much more fleshed out in the remake, expresses shock and immediate concern for the Deku Tree, while Saria is devastated at the thought of Link leaving Kokiri Forest. She leaves, heartbroken at Link’s decision, and it’s only when we exit the forest that she catches up to make amends and deliver the Fairy Ocarina.

This extra scene isn’t much in the grand scheme of things, but it really adds weight to Link’s departure, emphasising the home and friends that he’ll be leaving behind. I love it.

Difficult to remember because I only played Zelda Ocarina once back in the day, and revisiting it in recent years I was confronted with a blurring, clunky mess and barely lasted an hour in it. The remake is a godsend for someone like me eager to experience it again without suffering the many archaic elements that present themselves today.

I mostly notice that everything feels nicer. There's none of the clunkiness whether that be in the controls, obviously a vastly improved frame rate, and general design tweaks. One that I did note is the narrow path in the Fire Temple where a fall meant a long walk all the way back to trying it again. Boring! Now, Link will cling to the ledge and recover, or will fall into a lava pit, lose health, and respawn.

I bet this is one of the petty examples that IGN used to say this version of Ocarina is "easier" in its obvious agenda to not score it a 10. Whereas to sane people, the punishment from that fall is purely cheap game design. The path is easy to traverse as long as it's not rushed, so clinging to the ledge or losing health is an excellent two-stage warning to be careful compared to the previous brutal method after some simple carelessness. That is much more in sync with the ethos of Ocarina whereas in something like Ghosts N Goblins, that sort of cheap punishment is to be expected!

There are a lot of little things I like. Pro / Master HUD is great. Jumping changes gameplay. The cutscenes are astonishing, especially the scene you get the master sword for the first time. All great but the best? It’s the three C’s. Character, Camera, and Controls for me.

We take it for granted but dual sticks and 100% camera control makes such a fundamental difference in the gameplay that I truly believe it will surprise many how it feels to go back to play the original. It just gives me even more freedom. Ocarina of Time was the first game I played on N64. It was my first 3D game and introduced me to “open worlds”. To now experience that with modern camera controls with all the other changes just really seals the deal for me. Link does what I want, when I want it, and how I want. I never feel cheated. I feel like when I run up and jump near Epona, it just works and Link mounts correctly. I like when I walk around with my shield up, he keeps walking forward but I can pivot my shield to the left or right. I can control my sword swing direction. I can swing the camera just where I need it and it doesn’t clip into the environment. They way Link responds to all my inputs just feels… right.

A lot of people will go back to the original. It was will still hold up very well, but all things considered, the camera controls makes the biggest difference to me. I can say so far, this is my favourite version of Ocarina of Time and I am surprised I feel this way. This game beat my expectations.

If I had any minor criticisms about the controls, it’s simply the fact I can’t be as hardcore as in the N64 version, and I don’t have a separate dedicated button to raise my shield while Z-targeting like in the original version.

They nailed the feeling of walking on ice! The frosting and the snow in the Ice Cavern is amazing. Actually made me reach for a blanket!

#4188. Marathon launch player numbers are about half those of the Server Slam, at least on PC

Marathon hasn't quite been able to attract the same volume of players the recent Server Slam did.

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially launched. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually showed up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

In Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

Marathon has now officially launched, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

Indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

#4187. Ocarina of Time Remake Finally Gives Zelda’s Saddest Story the Attention It Deserves

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

After nearly 30 years, the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is finally here, and it's already winning over critics and fans alike – myself included. As I highlighted in my review, this new version embodies what a modern remake should be: an experience that embraces contemporary improvements without losing the old soul of the classic we all love!

And one of the things I've always loved about Ocarina of Time is how many curious characters are scattered throughout Hyrule. Some have surprisingly elaborate backstories, while others barely give you enough information to understand what's going on. More often than not, you need to be genuinely curious to piece together their stories and figure out what they're doing in the world.

My favorite example, by far, is Grog, a rather strange-looking punk who barely appeared in the original game but arguably had one of its saddest stories. Much of what made his character so fascinating came from the lovely fan theories surrounding his family and his mysterious disappearance.

To my surprise, the Switch 2 remake doesn't just subtly address some of those theories, but it also expands Grog's story in ways that make his already tragic arc considerably more meaningful. And to appreciate just how much has changed, we first need to revisit what made this little side story so memorable in the first place.

First things first, let's remember how Grog's story unfolded in the original Ocarina of Time. The character only appeared in two locations throughout the entire adventure: beneath a tree in Kakariko Village at night as Child Link, and later in the Lost Woods as Adult Link.

In Kakariko Village, you'll find him sitting beneath the tree in the center of town, looking rather miserable. Talk to him, and you'll quickly discover that he's not exactly the friendliest person around. He's withdrawn, bitter, and apparently hates just about everyone – including Link, simply for daring to approach him! And that's pretty much all you get from this first encounter.

To my surprise, the Switch 2 remake doesn't just subtly address some of those theories, but it also expands Grog's story in ways that make his already tragic arc considerably more meaningful.

His second appearance, however, is where things get interesting. As Adult Link, you can find Grog in the Lost Woods, but getting him to appear requires a little detour. First, you need to talk to the Cucco Lady in Kakariko Village, who turns out to be Grog's sister. She explains that he had a falling-out with their father, the village's Master Craftsman, and eventually left home. She's worried about him, though, so she gives you an egg that eventually hatches into Cojiro, Grog's beloved blue Cucco.

After using Cojiro to wake up Talon in Kakariko Village, you can take the Cucco into the Lost Woods. That's when you'll finally find Grog again, now seven years later, sitting in a rather strange, almost lifeless state. However, showing him Cojiro seems to snap him out of it, and he asks you to take an Odd Mushroom to the Granny's Potion Shop so she can prepare a medicine for him.

There's just one problem: when you return with the medicine, Grog is nowhere to be found. Instead, you're greeted by Fado, one of the Kokiri children, who explains that he disappeared into the Lost Woods. She also tells you that adults who get lost in the forest turn into Stalfos – those skeletal enemies that have been giving Link a hard time throughout the adventure.

And just like that, Grog's story appears to come to an end. The implication is pretty heartbreaking: the troubled young man who left home after a disagreement with his father has seemingly lost himself in the forest, never to return.

But even that brief story leaves plenty of unanswered questions. What exactly happened between Grog and his father? Why was he so unhappy? And what was the medicine supposed to cure? The original game never gave us definitive answers, leaving players to connect the dots through scattered dialogue and a handful of subtle clues. Thankfully, the remake finally gives us a much closer look at what was going on!

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

One of the most interesting additions in the remake is a new time system that allows the day-night cycle to progress naturally even while you're exploring towns and villages. Outside of more contained areas, such as dungeons and minigame shops, NPCs now follow their own schedules, appearing in different locations and going about their daily routines.

It's a relatively small change, but it makes Hyrule feel considerably more alive – and if you're a fan of Majora's Mask, you'll probably appreciate the familiar feeling of watching characters follow their own little agendas instead of simply standing around waiting for Link to show up!

Outside of more contained areas, such as dungeons and minigame shops, NPCs now follow their own schedules, appearing in different locations and going about their daily routines.

More importantly, this new system gives us additional opportunities to learn about Grog when playing as Child Link. For starters, you can now find him during the day near the entrance to Kakariko Village's graveyard. He's officially identified as the Master Craftsman's Son, making his connection to the village's grumpy carpenter much clearer from the beginning. Talk to him (or simply get close enough to hear him mumbling to himself) and you'll discover that his hatred for practically everything is closely tied to his strained relationship with his father.

And speaking of the Master Craftsman, the remake also gives us a better look at his daily routine. He and his assistants no longer spend all their time repeating the same actions in the same spots. Instead, they're spread throughout the village, and they even gather in front of the central tree for a meeting as the day comes to an end.

Talking to the assistants reveals that they also find their boss rather difficult to deal with. He's a grumpy, demanding man who seems to have a complaint about just about everything. Yet, interestingly enough, none of those complaints ever seem to involve Grog. While his son is clearly consumed by their strained relationship, the Master Craftsman barely acknowledges that anything is wrong – or just wants to ignore it.

But my favorite addition is that you can actually follow Grog around Kakariko Village throughout the day. He eventually gets up from his spot and sneaks behind a pile of bricks near the construction site overseen by his father. There, he quietly mutters that he needs to wait for the Master Craftsman to leave before he can go inside.

And when night finally falls, Grog makes his way back to the central tree, recreating the exact scene we remember from the original game. It's such a small sequence, but it adds an entirely new layer to his character. We no longer just see a miserable young man sitting beneath a tree. We see someone who is actively avoiding his father, seemingly unable to find a way to repair their relationship. And considering what we eventually learn about Grog, that little detail becomes even more heartbreaking.

The remake also expands Grog's story when playing as Adult Link, particularly through additional dialogue with his sister and mother. As in the original, you'll only encounter Grog in the Lost Woods once you reach the point in the Biggoron Sword side quest where Cojiro has turned blue. However, the Cucco Lady now has considerably more information to share about why her brother left home in the first place.

According to her, Grog didn't want to follow the family business. While their father expected him to become a carpenter, Grog wanted to work with animals, something he was particularly passionate about and apparently quite good at. The Master Craftsman strongly disapproved of this decision, and their disagreement eventually caused a complete breakdown in their relationship.

This is a pretty significant addition because it finally gives us a clearer picture of what happened between the two. Grog wasn't simply a rebellious young man who decided to leave home. He had his own dreams and interests, but his father couldn't accept that his son wanted a different future.

After hearing this, you can head into the Lost Woods and follow the original sequence. Grog is still there, seemingly trapped in the same strange state, and showing him Cojiro produces the same reaction as before. He snaps out of it and asks you to take the Odd Mushroom to the Granny's Potion Shop.

However, Granny also has a few new things to say! She confirms that Grog has been acting foolishly by distancing himself from his family, adding another perspective to the conflict. It's a small exchange, but it helps establish that this isn't just a disagreement between a father and son. So yes, the entire family has been affected by Grog's departure.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake has finally been released, and fans have already discovered several game-breaking glitches.

Unfortunately, things take the same tragic turn when you return to the Lost Woods with the medicine. Grog is gone, and Fado is waiting in his place. This time, however, the encounter is considerably more unsettling. She immediately notices the medicine's smell and desperately asks you to hand it over, offering a tool Grog left behind in exchange. Then, she explains that adults who enter the forest and lose their way, just like Grog apparently did, eventually turn into Stalfos.

But the story doesn't quite end there. You can return to Kakariko Village and talk to the Cucco Lady again, who provides even more information about her brother. She explains that she now takes care of the Cuccos because Grog left home after refusing to become a carpenter. In other words, her own life has also been shaped by the same family conflict that drove him away. And she’s also still hopeful that her brother is okay and will be back someday.

Finally, you can take the tool Grog left behind to the Master Craftsman, who is now waiting near the entrance to Gerudo Valley. He recognizes it as something he had given his son and explains that he had asked Grog to return it personally. Instead, his son apparently chose to send someone else to do the job.

It's a rather dismissive reaction, especially considering everything we've learned about their relationship. Even after Grog has disappeared, his father seems more concerned about the way he returned a tool than the fact that he may never see his son again.

What always fascinated me about Grog's story in the original Ocarina of Time was how much the game managed to communicate without ever explicitly explaining anything. It gave us scattered clues, brief conversations, and seemingly unrelated characters who slowly revealed their connections to one another. The rest was left to the players, who spent years discussing theories about Grog, his family, and what might have happened to him.

The remake takes those little pieces and finally puts them together. We now know exactly why Grog left home, what caused the rift with his father, and how his decision affected the rest of his family. And while the game still leaves some things open to interpretation, his story feels much more complete.

What I particularly love about this addition is that it doesn't try to turn Grog into some incredibly important character or give him an elaborate questline that changes the entire adventure. Instead, it simply gives more attention to a person who was already part of Hyrule, allowing us to understand the struggles that were always hiding behind his grumpy attitude.

And there's something genuinely sad about realizing that the Stalfos we encounter throughout the game might have once been people with their own dreams, families, and reasons for entering the forest. Grog's story makes that possibility feel much more personal. After all, he wasn't some nameless traveler who got lost. He was a young man who wanted to follow his own path, but never managed to find a way back home.

We now know exactly why Grog left home, what caused the rift with his father, and how his decision affected the rest of his family. And while the game still leaves some things open to interpretation, his story feels much more complete.

I also love how this expanded story fits into what makes Ocarina of Time so special! Hyrule isn't just a collection of locations for Link to explore, but a world filled with people whose lives continue beyond the moments when we interact with them. Sometimes, all it takes is a few extra lines of dialogue or a character walking to a different spot at sunset to make that world feel considerably richer.

Of course, I still have one personal theory I'd rather believe. Maybe Grog didn't actually turn into a Stalfos. Maybe he discovered the secret entrance to Termina, found his way to Clock Town, and eventually became the Cucco-loving man we meet in Majora's Mask. After all, if there's anyone who deserves a happy ending surrounded by the animals he loves, it's Grog. And after everything this remake has revealed about his family, I think I'll keep believing that version of the story.

From suspicious house designs to familiar songs, fans think they've found clues.

#4186. Nioh 3 patch finally makes summons useful in boss fights, brings free armour for everyone

There's a new Nioh 3 patch out in the wild, and it's one that any player who regularly summons in boss fights will really appreciate.

Team Ninja continues to work on Nioh 3. The developer has been releasing regular updates for the action RPG since its launch in early February. Earlier patches have addressed major bugs like healing item use inconsistencies, and more have arrived since to tackle various balance and loot-related issues.

Today’s patch, version 1.04, is a major one, coming in at well over 1GB. There’s plenty here worth getting excited about, so let’s dig in.

To begin with, this is the patch that adds the promised free armour sets for both Ninja, and Samurai. When Nioh 3 reached one million sales, Team Ninja said it would gift every player the Thunderous set in celebration, and the set’s two variants are now available in-game.

The more interesting side of the patch is, unsurprisingly, its change log. There appears to be a focus on online co-op and AI summons in this one, with various tweaks to the make the process more rewarding, and, in some cases, worthwhile.

The amount of Glory obtained when you complete a mission in multiplayer has been increased, regardless of which player was the host. The other major change mainly affects AI Benevolent Grave summons, making it so bosses will no longer target a single player for almost the entirety of the fight.

While summoning AI helpers has always been useful in Nioh 3, they didn’t always help in boss fights, specifically because the boss tended to focus on the player who summoned them, leaving the AI to run around eating AoE hits before dying.

Patch 1.04 makes a couple of welcome gameplay tweaks to the feel of combat. Ninjutsu, and Onmyo Magic will now hit their targets more consistently in situations where there’s a difference in elevation between the player and the enemy.

In the same vein, you’ll now be able to attack (quick/strong) right after jumping, which removes the pause that previously buffered the attack instead. This could mean even more air combos that don’t specifically require Martial Arts.

You can look forward to a couple of quality of life tweaks in this patch, too, such as the change that allows the game to automatically send any Sudama Soul Cores dropped by merchants to your item box. This happens from the second one onwards, which means you won’t have to pick half a dozen each time you go to sell a batch of items.

Speaking of the item box, the limit of forging materials has been increased for some of them. If you’ve been running Battle Scroll missions and Expeditions for gear, you’ll be happy to know that you can now exit the session from the main menu directly.

There’s plenty more to patch 1.04, including fixes and balance tweaks for several weapons, such as Samurai dual swords, odachi, and more for a few Ninja weapons, too. The patch also brings several bug fixes to the game.

You can read the full set of patch notes on Steam.

#4184. Grand Theft Auto VI Will Run At 30 FPS On All Consoles, But PS5 Pro Will Feature 'Improved Clarity' And Ray-Traced Shadows

Grand Theft Auto VI launches next week on Thursday, November 19, and you can preload the game on your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X/S starting today, Rockstar Games has announced. The studio has also revealed what kind of visuals players can expect on their respective consoles, making clear that regardless of where you play, GTA VI targets 30 FPS gameplay.

"Grand Theft Auto VI has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits to bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life – while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants," Rockstar writes in a blog post.

Rockstar Games also breaks down the different graphical settings available on PlayStation and Xbox consoles. On PS5 Pro, GTA VI will feature "improved clarity through PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) and ray-traced shadows only available on PlayStation 5 Pro." On PS5 and PS5 Pro, the game will include "high-fidelity haptic feedback" fully integrated into DualSense controllers and adjustable via accessibility settings, improved spatial rendering so all in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D audio, and improved load times, "making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles."

On Xbox consoles, Rockstar doesn't dive into performance; instead, it focuses on Xbox Cloud Gaming on Xbox Series X/S and Xbox One consoles, noting this feature will use Xbox Series S graphics settings.

GTA VI will also fully support Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox.

GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

For more, check out the song "Pusher" from the game's original score, then check out the GTA VI launch trailer. After that, check out this exclusive story about how GTA VI features over 170 animal species and another about its tropical storms and hurricanes.

#4183. Fable Quest Trailer Ratio’d And Compared To Dragon Age

Xbox has just released a new gameplay trailer for Fable showing one of the game’s quests, but it might not have been the best showcase since it’s being bombarded with dislikes.

Ever since the initial reveal trailer more than six years ago, Fable has easily been one of Xbox’s most highly anticipated games. That excitement has only increased with each gameplay showcase and trailer, which have shown just how far Playground Games has pushed the original trilogy’s mechanics, even if the reboot is leaving some things behind.

Of course, while most people are looking forward to Fable, it’s also been a target for online hate campaigns ever since the second trailer. Recent showings of Fable, including one that was focused on combat, have notably had a lot of backlash, and that drama has all come to a head with the latest trailer for the game.

Earlier this week, the official Fable YouTube account shared a new trailer for the game that highlights a quest where the Hero and Arden investigate what’s happening to Oakshire. The gameplay admittedly isn’t the most exciting thing in the world, since it mostly just shows the Hero walking through the area, getting in a fight, and talking to Arden before a big plot tease at the end.

Fable will let us hit on as many townsfolk as we want, but am I the only one who liked getting at least one proper romance option in Fable 3?

While it’s not a great showcase, the quest trailer is pretty harmless overall in my opinion and not that noteworthy. People don’t seem to agree with that, though, as the trailer is being ratio’d on YouTube with 4,200 dislikes compared to 3,400 likes as of the time of writing and an incredibly negative comments section with some brutal reactions.

One notable trend in the comments section is comparisons to Dragon Age: The Veilguard, with one popular comment calling it “Fable Age: The Veilguard”. Others are simply calling it out as a “disappointing” trailer that ended too soon and didn’t really show anything of substance. As one user puts it, “Is that really the best they can show?”

The Fable account is definitely seeing these negative comments too, as it’s heart-reacted the few positive ones praising the voice acting and graphics.

It’s not just the YouTube video that’s being slammed, either, as Xbox CEO Asha Sharma’s post about the trailer on Twitter is also full of backlash and the usual “Sweet Baby Inc” comments over two female characters. Some of it is clearly bad faith, but I’d be very hard-pressed to say the footage was worthy of a trailer.

It's been a long, hard road back to success for Sports Interactive, but FM 27 is the game I hoped it would be and so much more.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4182. The Sims 4 patch makes it so your public lot gatherings won't be interrupted by rogue Sims

Stranger Sims will no longer just crash your public lot events in The Sims 4 to talk about whatever.

The Sims 4 will soon get a new update to resolve a number of issues, some of which have long caused headaches for players. The latest update will arrive March 17 on PC and Mac, followed by PlayStation and Xbox at an unspecified time later.

Outside of the fixes themselves, the patch also makes good on the recent re-commitment to continue improving quality of life for players, so there’s plenty here longtime players will appreciate.

In the latest episode of The Sims 4’s Laundry List blog series, where the developer goes through the most reported problems with the game and how it plans to solve them, we got a rundown of what to expect from next week’s patch.

You can look forward to five major fixes in this one, but arguably the most important is a change to how Sims determine who they speak with on a lot. This is especially relevant for public lots, where Sims would sometimes interrupt ongoing conversations by barging in and starting a conversation with your Sim.

Going forward, Sims will prioritise familiar Sims with whom they already have rapport, and be less likely to latch onto strangers. If you’ve witnessed a date your Sim was on get interrupted because of that, you’ll certainly appreciate the change.

Speaking of budding romance, Prom is coming back to in-game Calendars, and Sims can once again attend. Maxis said this will work with new and existing saves, and that you should also expect Prom goals to be completable once again.

Pets and animals get some love in this patch, too. First, pets and horses will no longer get lost in Premade Households. The fix prevents that from happening in new saves, but if you already had that happen to you in your current save, it’ll still be there.

You may now also assign animals to an Animal Shed after moving your house to a new lot, so you hopefully won’t be confused as to why they’re stuck in your inventory. This fix applies to existing saves as well as new ones.

Lower down the list of urgent fixes is an update that makes it so Sims’ eye blinking will show fully closed eyes for most interactions. The upcoming patch also comes with a host of Sims autonomy fixes, including one that prevents them from excessively flirting with each other.

Catch up on the full list at the link near the top of the page. And, in case you missed it, Maxis recently announced that The Sims 4 will soon get paid mods, something that many in the community are skeptical about.

#4181. Update: You Can Preload Grand Theft Auto VI On PS5 and Xbox Today, And You Should Because It's Massive

Rockstar Games revealed last week that players can preload Grand Theft Auto VI on their console of choice the following week, and that time has arrived. The studio released a blog post today to announce that you can preload GTA VI on PlayStation 5, PlayStation 5 Pro, Xbox Series X, and Xbox Series S. If you're excited about the game, you will probably want to go ahead and do this because it will take up a whopping 212 GB of space on your drives – make the room now so you don't hit this roadblock next week when the game goes live on Thursday, November 19.

The blog post also details performance on PlayStation and Xbox consoles, and you can read more about what to expect here.

We're just over two weeks away from the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, which recently graced the cover of Game Informer. Ahead of its November 19 launch, Rockstar Games has announced that digital preloading for GTA VI will begin next week on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.

More specifically, preloading on Xbox Series X/S will begin Tuesday, November 10, at 12 a.m. GMT (4 p.m. PT/7 p.m. ET on November 9), and on PS5 at midnight local time in your time zone. Although Rockstar isn't producing physical discs of GTA VI, you can still buy a physical box at retail, which includes a download code for the game. The studio says, "Code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12."

The preload file will require 212 GB on your device, so make sure you have the space before you start the download. You can find more details about this process here.

Elsewhere in today's GTA VI news, Rockstar has revealed that on November 19, it will add an official printable GTA VI cover art poster and a map of Leonida as a free digital download to the game's official site. However, a double-sided physical version of this poster will be made available shortly after the launch of GTA VI from the Rockstar Store. It will only cost $0.99 on its own, or come free with any other purchase from the store.

GTA VI launches November 19 on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S.

#4180. 10 Great Games That Defined The Original Xbox

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

25 years ago, on November 15th, 2001, the gaming industry was forever changed when Microsoft officially dived into the console gaming market with the debut of its first home console, simply called the Xbox.

Designed to be a bridge between the hardware and software capabilities of PCs and the accessibility of home gaming consoles, the original Xbox console took the world by storm with its revolutionary gaming titles and services, proving that the United States can still rival Japanese gaming prospects.

With the original Xbox, and the overall Xbox brand, celebrating its momentous 25th anniversary this November, here’s a look back at 10 great exclusive games that defined the original Xbox and helped pave the way for Microsoft to become a modern gaming juggernaut.

Today, Xbox is largely known for three exclusive franchises: Halo, Gears of War, and Forza but long before the latter simulation racing series took the Xbox brand by storm during the Xbox 360 era, there was another series that stood as Xbox’s premier exclusive racing franchise: Project Gotham Racing.

Originally released as one of the Xbox’s many launch titles, the first Project Gotham Racing allowed up to four players in split-screen multiplayer to race against each other using 29 of the hottest cars of the early 21st century across San Francisco, London, Tokyo, and New York City.

With its stunt-focused Kudos point system and fun, arcade-like modes, Project Gotham Racing became one of the earliest Platinum Hits on the Xbox, leading to the development of three direct sequels, a few spinoffs, and the hit Xbox Live Arcade game, Geometry Wars.

Every great console needs its own standout amusing party game, and while Nintendo had Mario Party and PlayStation had Crash Bash, Xbox got its own distinct party game in the form of Fuzion Frenzy.

Another Xbox launch title, Fuzion Frenzy was an original party game not based on any prior IP, with the game being set in a futuristic tournament pitting four players against one another across randomized or pre-selected minigames with the goal of obtaining as many orbs and points as possible.

Chaotic minigames like Paint Panic and Falling Star quickly made Fuzion Frenzy a fan-favorite, and while it only got one sequel on the Xbox 360, many players still go back to play its wacky games to this very day (thanks to FF being backwards compatible on every future Xbox platform).

The sixth generation of consoles was a time for beginnings and a time for endings for many in the gaming industry at the time, most notably Sega. The Sega Dreamcast would mark the end for its home console prospects.

However, the failure of the Dreamcast didn’t mark the end for several Sega properties, as Microsoft collaborated with Sega to make the Xbox the exclusive home for several Dreamcast ports and sequels. Arguably the best was the funky Jet Set Radio Future.

A sequel to Jet Grind Radio, Jet Set Radio Future is a hyper stylized action game set in a futuristic Tokyo, where a group of teenagers called the GGs skate throughout the city and spray paint graffiti as a form of resistance against the dominating Rokkaku Group megacorporation.

Fans of the original Xbox who want play adventure titles that feature villains as protagonists should check out these 10 games

The RPG giant that is Bethesda is currently owned by Microsoft, and is a major part of Xbox’s future game investments. The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel is rumored to become a Project Helix exclusive, but long before Microsoft purchased Bethesda, the two companies first collaborated to release The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind exclusively on the original Xbox.

The first Elder Scrolls title to debut on a home console, The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind was a first and third-person RPG set in the titular ash-clouded Tamriel province of Morrowind, following a customizable prisoner who sets out on a journey to defeat the oppressive Dagoth Ur.

While Morrowind hasn’t aged as well as its successors, it paved the way for Bethesda to debut other landmark RPGs, such as Fallout, Skyrim, and Starfield on consoles, helping showcase the immense potential of western RPGs.

One of the greatest innovations the original Xbox featured was the creation of Xbox Live, as it was one of the first online multiplayer gaming services designed for home consoles and practically laid the groundwork for all modern online gaming services. Xbox Live’s debut title was MechAssault.

Set in the multimedia BattleTech franchise, MechAssault is a third-person mech shooter game set on the planet Helios. It follows a Wolf's Dragoons BattleMech pilot as they attempt to liberate the planet from the technology-worshipping faction Word of Blake.

MechAssault’s campaign is a lot of fun, but the game is far more famous for its multiplayer as it was one of the first console titles to feature Quick Matches, the ability to host and invite friends to online games, and multiplayer DLC such as new maps, gametypes, and new types of mechs like Raven and Loki.

Every sixth generation console featured fantastic titles that were beloved by many but just didn’t sell well enough to receive proper sequels, resulting in these types of games becoming cult classics. There’s no better Xbox cult classic out there than Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge.

Loosely based on the 1998 Crimson Skies board game, Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge has players embody Fortune Hunters air pirate gang leader Nathan Zachary, in an alternate 20th century where planes and zeppelins became the primary mode of transportation and the U.S. split into warring nations.

With an interesting world and story highly reminiscent of classic pulp books and films like Indiana Jones and enthralling third-person fighter plane gameplay, Revenge quickly became a fan-favorite. While it never received a sequel, it has since become the unofficial mascot for Xbox’s backwards compatibility.

These classic games will require some work to play again unless you have an older-gen console.

Early on in the Xbox brand’s history, Xbox’s most famous exclusive franchises were Halo, Gears of War, and Peter Molyneux's highly ambitious fantasy RPG Fable, which is finally set to return to Xbox early next year with a reboot of the series.

The original Fable was claimed by Molyneux to be the most ambitious RPG of the sixth console generation, with the game supposedly allowing players to have children in-game, play through the protagonist’s entire life, and witness plant life grow throughout the game, among other promises.

While most of these features weren’t present in the first Fable game, the original Fable still turned out to be an incredibly charming, comedic, and overall fun RPG, thanks to its witty British humor, morality system, and vast numbers of ways to interact with NPCs such as getting married and farting on people.

Nintendo fans recently got to take part in the midnight launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launch at various gaming stores. Those launch events paled in comparison to the cultural phenomenon that was the launch of Halo 2.

The original Xbox was arguably the house Halo: Combat Evolved built, and as such, most gamers in the world were excited to see how Bungie would improve upon the series in Halo 2, leading to the sequel receiving 1.5 million U.S. pre-orders and selling over 2.4 million copies in its launch day alone.

This anticipation was warranted though, as Halo 2 became the most popular Xbox Live game up until the release of Gears of War 1 and is widely regarded to feature one of the best FPS campaigns of all time thanks to the introduction of the Arbiter, dual-wielding, vehicle hijacking, and more.

The original Xbox was home to very few JRPGs, but these obscure ones might have something left exploring if you're interested.

While Fable 1 is the RPG most associated with the original Xbox, I would argue that it wasn’t the best RPG available on the console, with that honor instead going to BioWare’s epic 2003 masterpiece Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.

Many Star Wars video games were released exclusively for the original Xbox, but KOTOR was by far the most notable. It not only took place roughly 4,000 years before the events of the films during the Jedi Civil War, but featured one of the greatest gaming twists of all time, centered around Darth Revan.

KOTOR’s rather clunky round-based combat hasn't exactly aged well over the years, but its story and characters are still regarded as being some of the best to appear any RPG, such as Darth Malak, Jedi Knight Bastila Shan, the murderous droid HK-47, and the Mandalorian Canderous Ordo to name a few.

Finally, without a doubt, the number one exclusive video game that defined the original Xbox and arguably the Xbox brand overall was the launch title and Bungie’s revolutionary FPS Halo: Combat Evolved.

Halo: Combat Evolved was the definitive console-based FPS that truly showcased the capability of consoles to deliver an engaging, fun, and wondrous FPS experience, thanks to its cinematic quality, wide-open spaces, addictive gunplay and vehicle combat, and engrossing FPS multiplayer maps.

If Halo: Combat Evolved hadn’t been packaged with most Xbox consoles on day one, Xbox likely wouldn’t have lasted beyond the sixth generation of consoles and CE’s success ultimately led to Xbox not only obtaining a mascot with Master Chief but the creation of one of the most beloved sci-fi multimedia franchises of all time.

#4179. Crimson Desert PC specs don't keep resolution and framerate targets a secret, and they don't use upscaling for everything either

Finally, a PC specification list that actually indicates resolution and framerate targets, and doesn't leave console players behind.

Crimson Desert is a little over one week away from release, and developer Pearl Abyss has delivered the official, final list of specs for the game. The twist is that the specs not only include useful information for PC players, they also cover similarly relevant details for console players, who traditionally don’t get mentioned in those reveals.

The specs are decently detailed, but more surprisingly - except for a single instance - they don’t include upscaling on PC, another thing games have gotten too comfortable using, even with their lowest specs.

On the official Crimson Desert website, developer Pearl Abyss has delivered a chunky post breaking down five different sets of PC requirements for the upcoming open-world action RPG. Each set indicates the graphics preset being used - and crucially, the resolution and framerate targets you can expect with each.

With the exception of the Minimum spec, all other presets do not appear to rely on upscaling of any kind. They do not say, however, whether ray tracing is being used with any of them, which is a feature that will throw all of those specs out of whack.

That same transparency also extends to non-PC platforms, which traditionally get few, if any, details about their own resolution and framerate targets. The console set of specs are extensive, just like PC, covering both PlayStation, and Xbox.

It’s granular enough to indicate which upscaling tech is being used, where applicable. This is relevant for owners of a PS5 Pro, a console that has access to Sony’s PSSR upscaling, alongside the standard AMD FSR tech the base console - and Xbox - use.

The developer has also revealed the base resolution for each mode across each console, and the resolution the image will be upscaled to using whichever tech is being utilised.

And, if you’re one of the five people who play games on Mac, you’ll be thrilled to know that the specs also include a section for Mac devices, split between the different Mac chips. The quality preset being used with each is not clear, however.

Finally, there's a set of specs for the Rog Xbox Ally, covering both the X and S models.

Crimson Desert arrives March 20 on PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X/S. You can expect more coverage from us at release and beyond.

#4177. House House Discloses AI Use For 'Under 0.1%' Of Big Walk's Code Following IGF Voting Controversy

Big Walk developer House House has found itself at the center of a controversy over the upcoming Independent Games Festival on March 3, 2027, after a group of its jurors said they would not vote for any game that has used generative AI in any capacity. The jurors' statement does not name House House or Big Walk, but the studio eventually updated its FAQ to explain how it used generative AI for coding after IGF discussions. After vaguely posting on social media, those associated with IGF made clear that a sticking point in the voting process was Big Walk.

Former games journalist and game developer Austin Walker posted the IGF jurors' statement on Bluesky, explaining that voting has been difficult this year due to the "significant increase in the number of submitted games developed with generative AI tools."

"This has set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools, and at this point there is no universal consensus on what (if anything) is to be done," the statement reads. "The IGF has affirmed that we may cast our votes according to our own tastes and values. But we, as a contingent of IGF jurors, feel that this trend and the games embracing it deserve stronger pushback than a vote in silence."

The statement continues, explaining that not all jurors are on board with the blanket statement, citing reasons including "their ability to safely sign without professional blowback." It continues, "Above all: Our goal is to state solidarity with those who despair over the future of their art, their craft, and their industry – including those who have experimented with these tools, but who now believe they are not in our best interest."

The statement continues with the jurors' beliefs regarding gen-AI, including its negative effects, that any gen-AI used in any process of game development is not okay, noting specifically that "AI-generated code is not an exception to these harms," and more.

"For those reasons, this year we are declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity," the statement says. "We urge the IGF to adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work." The statement then includes the names of the IGF jurors who signed it.

Big Walk isn't specifically mentioned within that statement. However, Kyle LeClair, a four-time IGF judge and a juror for the upcoming IGF, tells Aftermath that "it got to the point where the most-discussed game this year almost entirely involved its AI usage, overshadowing pretty much everything else." LeClair says it felt like a boiling point, adding, "Anyhow, strong props to the jurors for taking this stance and putting out this letter as well, even if some people believe that using AI for coding purposes is a more gray area, we're at a point where the amount of AI slop clogging up the indie game scene means having to take hard stances such as this in order to discourage such an amount of recklessness."

Again, no mention of Big Walk. However, game developer Bruno Diaz took to BlueSky to confirm the speculation: that most-discussed game was Big Walk. "Okay, because the cat is out of the f---ing bag, I might as well combat misinformation a bit: 1. The reason IGF judges are aware of the LLM use in the development of Big Walk is through a disclosure shared by House House. 2. This disclosure was required by IGF rules. 3. While some have characterized the LLM usage as just fixing one individual blocking bug, this is a bit inaccurate; the description given by House House mentioned there being several instances, though they did also say it was mostly 'consultative' use and not code gen or agents."

Diaz notes that they believe that distinction is without a difference, adding that "to my knowledge, it is not the case that Big Walk is non-compliant with the former [Steam's AI disclosure requirements]."

"Yes, there was a large discussion about this in internal IGF forums," Diaz said. "Yes, a lot of people said things that I personally think were disingenuous, extremely disappointing, or just (frankly) dumb. No, I have no intention of talking about it in further detail or exposing anyone. [...] Ultimately, it is extremely difficult for a group of over 100 people to keep a secret so I expected this to come out eventually. Shrug emoji. If you think something is reputationally damaging, consider not doing it."

With discussion surrounding Big Walk happening during the IGF discussions, House House updated its FAQ to address, "Was AI used to make Big Walk?" Here's what the FAQ reads, in full:

"In the final stretch of Big Walk’s development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs. In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.

The primary use case for House House’s use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code. If you’re technically-minded, and curious, here’s an example. We needed to cull shadow casters by distance from the camera, but Unity URP only allows culling shadow casters by distance in camera forwards, so shadow casters behind the player were being rendered at an infinite distance. This made our game run 50% slower for around 20 seconds at sunrise and sunset. We researched the problem extensively, and we looked at the URP code ourselves, but we couldn’t find a way. Then, we were able to speak directly to an engineer at Unity, who asked around and ultimately concluded that what we wanted wasn’t possible. Finally, we posed the question to an LLM chatbot. After a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code inside URP.

We originally wrote a version of the above disclosure as it was a suggested part of our IGF submission. We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage. We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest.

This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.

Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

As you can see, House House did not disclose its use of AI-generated code because "Steam as a platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage." It says it is posting the disclosure now as "it has become a matter of public interest."

House House recently made headlines for choosing not to put Big Walk on Xbox in accordance with the Palestinian-led BDS boycott against Microsoft Games. Earlier this year, it gained widespread critical acclaim for its unique emphasis on cooperative puzzle-solving – you can read more about that in Game Informer's Big Walk review.

#4176. Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang Resigns Following Infidelity Scandal

Company produces custom processor for Switch 2

Nvidia, one of the largest tech firms in the world and the company responsible for the Switch 2's custom processor, has found itself embroiled in scandal over recent days.

As reported by The Guardian, Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, who you might recognise from the 'Creator's Voice Special Edition' video for Switch 2, has now resigned after reported affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee.

He will be replaced on an interim basis by Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, until a full-time successor is named. Nvidia's share price began to sharply decline following reports of the scandal, to the point where it is now no longer the most valuable company in the world.

The BBC speculates that Huang's departure could set him up to be a "formidable opponent" to the very company he co-founded, with Elon Musk stating that it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.

With regards to Nintendo, it's likely that none of this will have any immediate impact on Nvidia's relationship with the Japanese company. Nvidia will no doubt be under contract to supply custom chips for the Switch 2, but what happens with the inevitable Switch 2 successor is under question.

Hopefully everything will go smoothly for Nintendo, but if it wants to utilise Nvidia's architecture for its next console – particularly for backwards compatibility – then its efforts may be impacted by Huang's departure along with Nvidia's sharp pivot towards AI.

Of course, it's really early to be speculating about the 'Switch 3', but you can bet that Nintendo's R&D department will be looking at all of this very closely and considering its potential impact.
